# Urea OTS — As-Built Mathematical Reference

**Version 1.1** — the authoritative statement of every equation, correlation and thermodynamic
package the simulator runs on, and of **why each one was chosen over the alternatives**.

Scope: 1750 MTPD Stamicarbon-type CO2-stripping urea plant (Helwan Fertilizers Company).
Design basis: `References/Combined_1750_MTPD_100% load_PFD TablesProcess_Data.md`, 100 % load.

> **Maintenance rule (`Claude.md` §3).** This document is updated in the same session as the code.
> An equation that changes in `ureasim/` and not here is a defect. A `[PORTED]` tag below means the
> relation is live in V1.1 and covered by an equivalence test; `[V1]` means it is still only in
> `E:\Simulator\Urea Simulation\backend` (decision 165) and awaits porting.

---

## How to read this document

It is over 21 000 lines. **Never read it whole** (`Claude.md` §3a). Grep for the heading, then read
that section alone.

* **Order.** Parts 0 to XV state the standing mathematics by layer; Part XI is the port status
  register, one row a ported relation with the tolerance achieved. From Part XVI on the Parts follow
  the order of the work: the units as they were ported, then one Part a session. A later Part
  supersedes an earlier one on the same relation, so read the latest Part that names the tag.
* **List the Parts** (their titles are the table of contents):
  `grep -n "^# Part" "Urea OTS — As-Built Mathematical Reference.md"`
* **Find a section.** Sections are numbered Part.section, and `§CVII.4` is the heading `## CVII.4`:
  `grep -n "^## CVII\.4 " "Urea OTS — As-Built Mathematical Reference.md"`
* **Find a tag, a decision or a handoff item.** Its headings first, the full text only if they miss:
  `grep -n "^#.*322E002" ...`, then `grep -n "decision 142" ...`
* **Write.** A session appends one Part at the end, numbered from `project.md`'s Next free numbers.
  That Part is the one home of the session's equations, measurements and closures; `project.md`,
  `handoff.md` and the session log cite its sections and do not repeat them.

---

# Part 0 — Reading guide: the four rules

Every equation in this simulator obeys four rules. They are stated once, here, because they
explain nine-tenths of the design decisions that follow.

### Rule 1 — The design point is reproduced *by construction*, not by luck

The plant has a licensor heat-and-mass balance (the PFD tables). The simulator must reproduce it
**bit-exactly** at 100 % load, or every downstream initialisation drifts. So wherever a correlation
is used to supply a *trend*, it is wrapped in a **departure (ratio) form** anchored at design:

$$
\phi_{\text{live}} \;=\; \phi_{\text{PFD}} \cdot \frac{\phi_{\text{model}}(\text{live state})}{\phi_{\text{model}}(\text{design state})}
$$

At the design state the bracket is exactly 1, so $\phi_{\text{live}} = \phi_{\text{PFD}}$ to the last
bit. Off design, the model supplies only the **derivative** — how the quantity moves. A systematic
offset in an extrapolated model **cancels identically** in that ratio; its slope does not, and the
slope is what a frozen constant reported as exactly zero.

This is why an imperfect activity model is still worth having. A model that is 3.6× low in absolute
bubble pressure but correct in its response to N/C ratio is *useful*; a hardcoded split vector that
is exactly right at design and has zero derivative is *useless for training*.

### Rule 2 — A model that leaves its fitted envelope must **refuse**, not extrapolate

The worst failure mode in this codebase's history was a table lookup that **clamped** at its edge
instead of failing. An out-of-envelope call then returned a frozen constant from behind a call that
looked like a rigorous solve — strictly worse than an honest hardcoded number, because the
heuristic became invisible.

Therefore: `classify()` returns `None` and `flash()` raises `OutOfDomain` whenever the state leaves
the tabulated envelope, and the caller keeps whatever anchored model it has. **Refusal is a
feature.**

### Rule 3 — Every consequence is a *rate*, never a *state override*

`if level <= 0: P = 1.013` is a step change in the right-hand side of an ODE. It chatters, it
cannot be undone by correct operator action (the state was overwritten, not driven), and it arrives
with zero transport lag no matter how far downstream the affected equipment sits.

Every deviation consequence enters as a **rate** that an existing balance integrates. The plant
recovers when the operator recovers it. That is the whole point of a training simulator.

### Rule 4 — No number without provenance

Every constant carries the document it came from. Where a number had to be back-solved from the
licensor duty (control-valve $C_v$, Onda's $c_i$, the reactor's $X_\infty$), the back-solve is
stated explicitly, together with what it does *not* give you.

# Part I — Thermodynamic package selection, and why

## I.1 The problem: one plant, four incompatible thermodynamic regimes

| Regime | Where | State | Why one model cannot cover it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pure water / steam** | 329 headers, every steam-heated shell, every condensate leg | 1–25 bar a, 100–225 °C | Needs an industrial-grade steam table, not a correlation |
| **Concentrated electrolyte** | 323 LP recirculation, 328 desorption, 322C001 absorber | 0.46–4.1 bar a, 45–200 °C, NH3 + CO2 + carbamate in water | Speciating electrolyte with ionic strength effects |
| **Near-binary urea melt** | 324E001 / 324E003 evaporators | 0.131–0.33 bar a, 130–140 °C, 94–99.7 wt% urea | Water is the *trace*; electrolyte molality basis diverges |
| **Supercritical-ish HP loop** | 322R001 / 322E001 / 322E002 / 322E003 | 140–145 bar a, 165–185 °C, $x_{H_2O} = 0.047$ | Outside every published fit for this system |

No single package covers all four. Pretending otherwise is how simulators acquire silent frozen
constants. The design **dispatches on composition** and is explicit about which model owns which
region.

## I.2 The packages, and the case for each

### I.2.1 IAPWS-IF97 (R7-97, 2012 revision) — pure water and steam

**Used for:** the 329 steam network, every steam-heated shell (322 / 323 / 324 / 328), every
condensate leg, and as the *water reference line* inside the activity models.

**Why:** it is the international industrial standard, its coefficients are published (nothing is
regressed here), and it supplies Region 4 (saturation), Region 1 (compressed/saturated liquid) and
Region 2 (vapour) — exactly the three the plant needs.

**What it replaced:** an Antoine saturation correlation (`tsat_steam` / `psat_water_bara`). Antoine
is fine near its fit range and wrong outside it; more importantly, having *two* water reference
lines (one in the steam system, one inside the VLE) guarantees the two will disagree. Now there is
one line and every module imports it.

**Envelope:** Region 1 valid to $T \le 623.15$ K. The plant's hottest water is the 25 bar a
battery-limit steam at ~224 °C — comfortably inside.

### I.2.2 Extended UNIQUAC (Thomsen & Rasmussen 1999; Darde et al. 2010/2011) — the electrolyte

**Used for:** the NH3-CO2-H2O liquid phase everywhere the volatiles carry the bubble point — the
323 recirculation train, 328 desorption/hydrolysis, and the 322C001 absorber.

**Why this model and not, say, Pitzer or e-NRTL:**

1. **Envelope match.** Validated 0–150 °C, 1–100 bar, to 100 molal NH3 — the exact envelope of the
   Unit-328 desorption train, Unit-324 vacuum condensers and the LP absorbers.
2. **It speciates.** The liquid carries NH3(aq)/NH4⁺/NH2COO⁻ and CO2(aq)/HCO3⁻/CO3²⁻ through the
   R1–R5 equilibria. A urea plant's LP section *is* carbamate chemistry; a model that lumps total
   NH3 cannot represent a desorber at all.
3. **It gives excess enthalpy and heat capacity directly**, from the same parameter set — so the
   energy balance and the phase equilibrium cannot drift apart.
4. **Its parameters are published in the open literature** and are transcribable verbatim. Nothing
   in the property layer is fitted in-house.

**Provenance (all verbatim, none fitted here):**

| Parameter group | Source |
|---|---|
| $u^0_{ij}$, $u^T_{ij}$, $r_i$, $q_i$, NH2COO⁻ heat capacity, fitted formation energies | Darde, PhD thesis, DTU 2011, Tables 2-2…2-6; published as Darde, van Well, Stenby, Thomsen, *Ind. Eng. Chem. Res.* **49** (2010) 12663 |
| Base-species Helgeson $C_p$ coefficients | Thomsen, PhD thesis, DTU 1997, Table 5.7 |
| $\Delta G_f^\circ$, $\Delta H_f^\circ$ at 298.15 K | CODATA / NIST |
| Henry constants NH3, CO2 in water | Rumpf & Maurer (1993), as Darde eqs 2.12–2.13 |
| Debye–Hückel term | Thomsen (2005) *IUPAC Pure Appl. Chem.* **77**, 531, eqs 6–9 ($b = 1.5$) |
| $C_p^\circ$(NH3 aq) = 72.04, $C_p^\circ$(CO2 aq) = 238.05 J/mol/K | Correa, Thomsen, Fosbøl, *Fuel* **335** (2023) 126863, Table 1 (open access) |

The $r,q$ transcription is **cross-checked against an independent second source**
(`References/Resolving Simulator Thermodynamics Gaps.docx`, Table 1) — exact match on all nine
species.

**Honest limitation, stated where it matters:** the interaction parameters are a *CO2-capture* set
regressed on dilute aqueous loadings below ~150 °C. At $x_{H_2O} = 0.047$ and 183 °C (the HP loop)
they are extrapolated hard. The measurement that says so: the model puts the 322R001 overflow bubble
pressure at **40.4 bar a** at 183 °C against a loop that runs at **144.2** — a factor 3.6 low.
**The engine never uses that absolute number.** Every 322 split runs on the Rule-1 ratio form.

### I.2.3 Neutral UNIQUAC, H2O/urea binary (Voskov & Voronin 2016) — the melt

**Used for:** 324E001 and 324E003, where the liquor is 94–99.7 wt% urea.

**Why a second liquid model at all:** urea is not a UNIQUAC species in the electrolyte parameter
set — it enters only as a mole-fraction diluent. At 94–98 wt% urea that assumption fails hard:

| stage | T (°C) | $P_{\text{PFD}}$ (bar a) | electrolyte error | neutral-hybrid error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 323C003 | 135 | 4.10 | +7.0 % | — (electrolyte used) |
| 323F004 | 106 | 1.13 | +17.5 % | — (electrolyte used) |
| 323F010 | 99 | 0.46 | +1.7 % | — (electrolyte used) |
| **324E001** | 130 | 0.330 | **+30.6 %** | used instead |
| **324E003** | 140 | 0.131 | **+65.7 %** | **+2.2 %** |

Two neutral species means the Debye–Hückel term is *identically zero*, so this **is** Extended
UNIQUAC in the urea/water limit — and it is the only one of the two that sees urea as a UNIQUAC
species rather than a diluent.

**Provenance:** equations, structural parameters and interaction convention transcribed from the
open supplementary implementation of Voskov & Voronin, *Thermodynamic model of the urea synthesis
process*, DOI 10.1021/acs.jced.6b00557 (`GRT_UNIQUAC.m`, `liquid_hc.m`, `liquid6comp.cpp`; X11/MIT
licence). Binary parameters: H2O→urea $(a_0, a_1) = (0, 0)$; urea→H2O $(-211.9567785927018\ \text{K}, 0)$.

**Declared extrapolation:** published validation envelope is 408.15–503.15 K and 35–450 bar a. Unit
324 runs 372.15–473.15 K at 0.02–1.00 bar a. This is therefore **classified as a design-anchored
extrapolation** in code, not silently used. Water fugacity comes from the shared IAPWS-IF97 line, not
from a private Antoine.

### I.2.4 Soave–Redlich–Kwong, $k_{ij} = 0$ — the vapour phase

**Used for:** vapour fugacity coefficients $\varphi_i^V$ in every $\gamma$–$\varphi$ flash, and for
the residual enthalpy in the HV-322604 isenthalpic letdown.

**Why:** Thomsen (2005) uses SRK with $k_{ij} = 0$ for this system, so pairing it with the Extended
UNIQUAC liquid keeps the $\gamma$–$\varphi$ formulation internally consistent with the source that
fitted the liquid. Critical constants are public NIST/DIPPR values.

**Why not an activity-only (ideal-gas) treatment:** at 140 bar a in the HP loop and for a letdown
across a 0.028 pressure ratio, the vapour is not ideal, and the residual enthalpy term is what makes
the Joule–Thomson result composition-dependent instead of a constant K/bar.

### I.2.5 H0 absolute enthalpy on an elements-at-298.15 K datum

**Used for:** every stream enthalpy, every energy balance, and to make `flash_PH` possible at all.

**Why a formation datum and not a sensible-only enthalpy:** decompose exactly,

$$
H_{\text{stream}} \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_i n_i\, h_i(T)}_{\text{formation + sensible + phase}} \;+\; \underbrace{H^E(T,x)}_{\text{mixing non-ideality}}
$$

Because every $h_i$ is referenced to its **elements** at 298.15 K / 1 bar (that is what a formation
enthalpy *is*), the first sum is **reaction-consistent by construction**: a reaction's enthalpy is
the difference of its members' formation enthalpies, so H0 does not create or destroy energy across
a reacting node. A sensible-only enthalpy does, which is why sensible-only was refused.

**The declared-tier scheme** — every stream carries a basis flag:

| tier | content | availability |
|---|---|---|
| **H0** | formation + sensible + phase reference, ideal solution ($H^E = 0$) | **live now** |
| H1 | H0 + $H^E$ from the tier's activity model | lands with each activity tier |
| H2 | H1 reconciled against the licensor heat balance | after the licensor point |

H0 is usable for heat balances and duty/trend estimates; it is **not** design-grade inside a
strongly non-ideal liquid, and the flag makes that honest per stream rather than a footnote.

**Provenance:** aqueous/ionic species reuse the *same* formation enthalpies and Helgeson $C_p(T)$
already validated in the property module (imported, not re-transcribed, so the two cannot diverge).
Ideal-gas formation enthalpies from CODATA Key Values / NIST-JANAF. Urea and biuret from Tischer et
al., *Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys.* **21** (2019) 16785 (open access). Heat-capacity coefficients
(Berman–Brown $a + eT^{-1/2}$) and **ammonium carbamate** formation enthalpies (solid −645.05,
liquid −624.32 kJ/mol) from Voskov & Voronin, *J. Chem. Eng. Data* **61** (2016) 4110, Table 1.

Carbamate's explicit formation enthalpy is what makes the loop enthalpy reaction-consistent
*through the carbamate node*, not merely across the net $2\,\mathrm{NH_3 + CO_2 \rightarrow urea + H_2O}$.

**Cross-check against this plant's own licensor manual** (Uhde UD-VT-G00-DC-0003,
`References/Sources/02 FUNDAMENTALS.pdf`): the elements datum reproduces the manual's reaction
enthalpies — carbamate step ≈ −159 kJ/mol (gas reactants) / −117 (condensed reactants, the plant's
figure) and urea step +18.8 kJ/mol against the plant's +15.5 — and the plant's urea remelt heat
15.1 kJ/mol brackets the Tischer fusion value 13.9 used here. All inside the H0 declared band.

### I.2.6 The empirical fallback layer

**Used for:** fast inner-loop calls where a rigorous solve is unaffordable at 10 Hz, and as the
comparison oracle during migration.

**Why it still exists:** a 10 Hz training simulator cannot run a speciating Newton solve at every
node every tick. The empirical layer carries anchored correlations for solution $c_p$, density and
bubble point; the rigorous layer supplies the *derivative* those anchors are scaled by. Keeping the
oracle also means any migration regression is measurable rather than argued.

## I.3 Domain dispatch — the decision that is not a fudge

```
classify(composition, T, P)
    ├── volatiles carry the bubble point ......... DOMAIN_ELECTROLYTE
    │       water activity from the electrolyte table
    │       → 323 recirculation / flash train, 328 desorption, 322C001
    ├── near-binary urea/water melt, volatiles are traces ... DOMAIN_NEUTRAL_UREA
    │       water activity from the neutral binary
    │       trace NH3/CO2 still from the electrolyte path (its dilute limit, well behaved)
    │       → 324E001, 324E003
    └── outside every tabulated envelope ......... None  →  flash() raises OutOfDomain
            caller keeps its anchored model
```

Dispatching on composition is not a fudge — it is the only honest reading of what each model was
fitted to.

## I.4 Why the HP loop grid is indexed in mole fractions, not molalities

The first activity table was indexed by $(T, N, C)$ with $N, C$ the total NH3 and CO2 loading in
**mol per kg of water**. That is the natural coordinate of a molality-referenced electrolyte model,
and it is fine everywhere water is the solvent. In the HP synthesis loop it is not a coordinate at
all:

| stage | T (°C) | $N$ (mol/kg water) | $C$ (mol/kg water) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 322R001 overflow (stream 207) | 183 | 100.0 | 22.4 |
| 322E003 off-gas feed | 183 | **869.3** | **258.1** |

…against a table that stopped at $N = 16$, $C = 7$. Those are not large numbers because the liquor
is exotic — they are large because **the denominator is vanishing**. The molality of a liquor with
no water in it is infinite, so *no* molality grid can ever be wide enough, and every finite one
silently clamps (Rule 2's exact failure mode).

In mole fractions the same two states are unremarkable:

| stage | $x_{\mathrm{NH_3}}$ | $x_{\mathrm{CO_2}}$ | $x_{\mathrm{H_2O}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 322R001 overflow | 0.562 | 0.126 | 0.312 |
| 322E003 off-gas feed | 0.735 | 0.218 | 0.047 |

So the grid is indexed by two **bounded** coordinates on the water + volatile sub-system:

$$
s = \frac{n_{\mathrm{NH_3}} + n_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{n_{\mathrm{NH_3}} + n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} + n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}} \in [0,1), \qquad
f = \frac{n_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{n_{\mathrm{NH_3}} + n_{\mathrm{CO_2}}} \in [0,1]
$$

**The evidence that this is a coordinate transform and not a new model:** on the re-indexed grid the
three 323 stages move by under one percentage point, and at two of the three they move *toward* the
plant (4.387→4.352, 1.328→1.299, 0.468→0.468 bar a).

Two further blockers were removed at the same time, and both were solver problems, not domain
limits:

* **Solver basin.** `speciate` stopped converging above $N \approx 40$ mol/kg water — a
  basin-of-attraction failure of its dilute initial guess. Seeded from a converged neighbour, the
  *identical* solver reaches $N = 869$ in five Newton steps at a residual of $8.5\times10^{-14}$.
  Every node of the rebuilt table is a converged solve (1215/1215); any node that were not would be
  stored with its flag cleared so the interpolator refuses cells touching it.
* **Inerts.** N2, O2, CH4 and H2 now carry SRK critical constants and IAPWS G7-04 Henry constants,
  so the loop's four permanent gases generate real K-values instead of forcing a refusal.

# Part II — The property layer

## II.1 IAPWS-IF97 `[V1: iapws_if97.py]` → `[ureasim/thermo/iapws.py]`

Region 4 saturation (forward and backward), Region 1 liquid, Region 2 vapour. Published R7-97
coefficients. Specific gas constant $R = 0.461526$ kJ/(kg·K).

Exports used by the plant model: $T_{\text{sat}}(P)$, $P_{\text{sat}}(T)$, $h_f$, $h_g$, latent heat
$\lambda$, saturated liquid density, saturated vapour specific volume.

**Process utility:** fixes every steam-heated shell temperature, every condensate enthalpy, and the
water reference line the activity models depart from.

## II.2 NH3-CO2-H2O property basis `[V1: props_nh3co2h2o.py]` → `[ureasim/thermo/properties.py]`

### II.2.1 Standard-state thermodynamics

Helgeson-form heat capacity:

$$
C_p^\circ(T) \;=\; a + bT + \frac{c}{T - 200}
$$

with $(a,b,c)$ per species from Thomsen 1997 Table 5.7. NH3(aq) and CO2(aq) enter in the
**constant-$C_p$ limit** ($a = C_p^\circ$, $b = c = 0$) from Correa et al. 2023 — exactly as NH4⁺ was
already treated.

*Process utility:* gives reaction equilibrium constants their temperature dependence, which is what
makes a desorber respond to steam rate instead of to a lookup.

### II.2.2 Liquid speciation — reactions R1–R5

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R1:}&& \mathrm{H_2O} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H^+ + OH^-} \\
\text{R2:}&& \mathrm{NH_4^+} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH_3(aq) + H^+} \\
\text{R3:}&& \mathrm{CO_2(aq) + H_2O} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{HCO_3^- + H^+} \\
\text{R4:}&& \mathrm{HCO_3^-} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CO_3^{2-} + H^+} \\
\text{R5:}&& \mathrm{NH_2COO^- + H_2O} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH_3(aq) + HCO_3^-}
\end{aligned}
$$

solved by **damped log-space Newton–Raphson** on the molality basis, subject to the N/C element
balances and the charge balance, with the *full* activity coefficients in the reaction quotients:

$$
K_j(T) \;=\; \prod_i a_i^{\nu_{ij}}, \qquad a_i = m_i \gamma_i
$$

Validation: every balance and reaction quotient closes to ~$10^{-10}$.

*Process utility:* the free-NH3 and free-CO2 back-pressure over a liquor **is** what a desorber
strips, what an absorber takes up, and what sets a bubble point. Nothing in the LP section is
representable without it.

### II.2.3 Activity coefficients — complete Extended UNIQUAC

$$
\ln \gamma_i \;=\; \underbrace{\ln \gamma_i^{C}}_{\text{combinatorial}} \;+\; \underbrace{\ln \gamma_i^{R}}_{\text{residual}} \;+\; \underbrace{\ln \gamma_i^{DH}}_{\text{Debye–Hückel}}
$$

* **Combinatorial** (Flory–Huggins + Staverman–Guggenheim) from $r_i$, $q_i$.
* **Residual** from $\Psi_{ij} = \exp[-(u_{ij} - u_{jj})/T]$ with $u_{ij} = u^0_{ij} + u^T_{ij}(T - 298.15)$.
* **Extended Debye–Hückel**, Thomsen (2005) eqs 6–9, with $b = 1.5$ and

$$
I = \tfrac12 \sum_i m_i z_i^2, \qquad
\ln\gamma^{DH}_i = -z_i^2 \frac{A\sqrt{I}}{1 + b\sqrt{I}}
$$

Symmetric convention for water, **unsymmetric** (infinite-dilution-referenced) for solutes, per
Thomsen (2005) eqs 17–18.

Validation: reproduces eqs 8/9 and the Debye–Hückel limiting law, and satisfies Gibbs–Duhem.

### II.2.4 Vapour fugacity — SRK

$$
Z^3 - Z^2 + (A - B - B^2)Z - AB = 0, \qquad A = \frac{a_m P}{R^2T^2},\; B = \frac{b_m P}{RT}
$$

with van der Waals mixing, $k_{ij} = 0$. Validated to approach ideal-gas at low $P$.

### II.2.5 Henry's law

NH3 and CO2: Rumpf & Maurer (1993), mole-fraction scale (Darde eqs 2.12–2.13).
N2, O2, CH4, H2: **IAPWS G7-04** — added so the loop's permanent gases produce real K-values.

### II.2.6 Reaction and excess enthalpy

$\Delta H_{\text{rxn}}$ explicit from formation enthalpies; $H^E$ from the temperature derivatives
of the model. Validated against textbook aqueous values (+55.8 / −52.2 / +14.9 kJ/mol).

## II.3 Aqueous solution bulk properties `[V1: main.py]` → `[ureasim/thermo/empirical.py]`

Anchored departure forms — a design anchor times a model ratio (Rule 1):

$$
c_p(w_{\text{urea}}, T) = c_{p,\text{anchor}} \cdot \frac{c_p^{\text{raw}}(w, T)}{c_p^{\text{raw}}(w_{\text{des}}, T_{\text{des}})}, \qquad
\rho(w_{\text{urea}}, T) = \rho_{\text{anchor}} \cdot \frac{\rho^{\text{raw}}(w, T)}{\rho^{\text{raw}}(w_{\text{des}}, T_{\text{des}})}
$$

*Process utility:* a urea solution's $c_p$ falls and its density rises as it concentrates from 68 %
to 99.7 % through the recirculation and evaporation train. A single constant $c_p$ would make every
evaporator duty wrong in the same direction, and the error would be invisible because the design
point would still close.

# Part III — The unified VLE / flash service

`[V1: thermo_service.py + vle_nh3co2h2o.py]` → `[ureasim/thermo/service.py + vle.py]`

## III.1 What it exposes

`flash()`, `flash_ph()`, `bubble_p()`, `bubble_t()`, `dew_t()` — one entry point for every phase
boundary in the flowsheet.

## III.2 The bubble-point equation

$$
P_{\text{bub}}(T) \;=\; f_{\text{dil}} \Big[\, a_{\mathrm{NH_3}} H_{\mathrm{NH_3}}(T) + a_{\mathrm{CO_2}} H_{\mathrm{CO_2}}(T) + a_{\mathrm{H_2O}} P^{\text{sat}}_{\mathrm{H_2O}}(T) \,\Big] \;+\; \sum_{j \in \text{inerts}} x_j H_j(T)
$$

where

* $a_i = x_i \gamma_i$ — activities from the full Extended UNIQUAC $\gamma$, on the R1–R5 speciation;
* $H_i$ — Rumpf & Maurer for NH3/CO2, IAPWS G7-04 for the permanent gases;
* $P^{\text{sat}}_{\mathrm{H_2O}}$ — IAPWS-IF97;
* $f_{\text{dil}}$ — urea and biuret are **non-volatile** and are not in the electrolyte parameter
  set, so they enter the only way they physically can at this concentration: as a **mole-fraction
  diluent** on every partial pressure.

$f_{\text{dil}}$ is the same Raoult-on-the-non-volatiles term the empirical `bubble_T_raoult` uses
for the urea-only stages, so **the two bubble-point models agree in the limit where the volatiles
vanish** — which is the consistency check that matters at the boundary between the 323 and 324 domains.

## III.3 What this replaced, and the size of the error

The live engine previously used `tsat_steam(P)` — a **pure-water** Antoine line with a frozen offset
— for the 323C003 and 323F004 bubble points, with a comment conceding the point in writing.

At the 323C003 design state the pure-water saturation temperature at 4.1 bar a is **144 °C**; the
column actually runs at **135 °C**. The 9 °C gap is the NH3 and CO2 partial pressure the water-only
model cannot see.

Worse than the offset — which the departure form absorbs — is the **slope**: a water-only anchor
makes the bubble point respond *only to pressure*, so a change in the liquor's NH3 or CO2 loading,
which is what every stripping, absorption and recycle upset in this plant does, moved the bubble
point by **exactly zero**.

## III.4 Validation — no fitted parameter anywhere in the chain

Evaluated on the engine's own composition vectors, through the tabulated-and-interpolated path the
engine actually calls:

| stage | liquor (PFD mass %) | T (°C) | $P_{\text{model}}$ | $P_{\text{PFD}}$ | error |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 323C003 | 68.74 U / 0.36 B / 2.13 N / 1.05 C | 135 | 4.3516 | 4.10 | +6.1 % |
| 323F004 | 71.74 U / 0.37 B / 0.88 N / 0.66 C | 106 | 1.2993 | 1.13 | +15.0 % |
| 323F010 | 80.00 U / 0.42 B / 0.08 N / 0.02 C | 99 | 0.4683 | 0.46 | +1.8 % |

Three stages spanning 0.46–4.1 bar a and 99–135 °C, from first principles.

**Why 323F004 is the loosest:** it is the stage where the CO2 term dominates, and CO2 is where this
model is weakest — at 0.66 wt% CO2 the carbamate equilibrium is steep, and urea (72 % of the liquor)
is a *diluent* here, not a UNIQUAC species, so it dilutes the volatiles without shifting their
activity coefficients. Tracked as **handoff B-2**.

**Why the offsets are acceptable:** every call site uses the **departure form**
$T_{\text{des}} + [T_{\text{bub}}(\text{live}) - T_{\text{bub}}(\text{design})]$, so the residual
cancels identically at the design point. For comparison, the pure-water anchor gives 103.3 °C at
323F004's 1.13 bar against an actual 106 °C — and responds to composition with a derivative of
exactly zero.

## III.5 Flash — Rachford–Rice on $\gamma$–$\varphi$ K-values

$$
\sum_i \frac{z_i(K_i - 1)}{1 + \beta(K_i - 1)} = 0, \qquad
K_i = \frac{\gamma_i\, \mathcal{H}_i \ \text{or}\ \gamma_i P_i^{\text{sat}}}{\varphi_i^V P}
$$

**Basis conventions that must not be lost in the port:**

* Compositions in and out are **mass fractions** over the engine species list; internals work in
  mole fractions.
* K-values are **apparent**, on a **total-species** basis. The electrolyte model speciates ammonia
  into NH3(aq)/NH4⁺/NH2COO⁻ and CO2 into CO2(aq)/HCO3⁻/CO3²⁻, but the flowsheet mass balance tracks
  *total* NH3 and *total* CO2. So

$$
K_i = \frac{p_i}{\varphi_i^V P\, x_{i,\text{total}}}
$$

  is the ratio the flowsheet needs, and it is the ratio the service returns.
* Urea, biuret and HCHO are non-volatile: $K = 0$ **exactly**.

## III.6 The anchored-ratio K-value — how the HP loop is handled

$$
\alpha_{\text{live}} = \alpha_{\text{PFD}} \cdot \frac{\alpha_{\text{model}}(\text{live})}{\alpha_{\text{model}}(\text{reference})}
$$

The licensor's absolute split is preserved **bit-exactly** at the design point, and the model
supplies only the derivative. This is Rule 1 applied where the fit is weakest, and it is the reason
a 3.6×-low absolute bubble pressure is not fatal.

---

# Part IV — Reaction kinetics and equilibrium

## IV.1 322R001 urea reactor — Modified Inoue–Kanai `[V1: reactor.py]` → `[ureasim/units/synthesis/reactor.py]`

**Chemistry.** Two steps, the first fast and exothermic, the second slow and endothermic:

$$
\mathrm{2\,NH_3 + CO_2 \rightleftharpoons NH_2COONH_4} \quad (\Delta H < 0, \text{ fast})
$$
$$
\mathrm{NH_2COONH_4 \rightleftharpoons NH_2CONH_2 + H_2O} \quad (\Delta H > 0, \text{ slow, rate-controlling})
$$

**Separable equilibrium structure** (re-fitted to plant HMB — *not* a transcription of published
Inoue–Kanai polynomial coefficients):

$$
X(L, W, T) \;=\; \min\big[\, X_\infty \cdot f_L(L) \cdot f_W(W) \cdot f_T(T),\; X_\infty \,\big]
$$

$$
f_L(L) = \frac{a(L-2)}{1 + a(L-2)}, \qquad
f_W(W) = \frac{1}{1 + bW}, \qquad
f_T(T) = \exp\!\big[-k\big((T - T_{\text{opt}})^2 - (T_0 - T_{\text{opt}})^2\big)\big]
$$

with $L = \mathrm{N/C}$ molar, $W = \mathrm{H/C}$ molar, and
$T_{\text{opt}}(L) = \operatorname{clip}(185 + 2(L-2),\, 185,\, 195)$ °C.

**Why each term has the shape it has:**

* $L = 2$ is the dehydration stoichiometric floor ($2\,\mathrm{NH_3} + \mathrm{CO_2} \rightarrow$
  urea $+\ \mathrm{H_2O}$). Excess NH3 drives the second step forward and **saturates** at high $L$ —
  hence the Langmuir-like form, not a power law.
* Product and recycle water **back-shift** the dehydration equilibrium — the H/C "water penalty" the
  whole stripping loop is sensitive to (Stamicarbon).
* $T_{\text{opt}}$ rises with $L$ because excess NH3 drives the *endothermic* dehydration step. At
  design $L_0$, $T_{\text{opt}} \approx 187$ °C, so the design $T_0 = 183$ °C sits on the **rising
  flank**, below the peak — which is why the reactor responds to a temperature rise the way the
  plant does.

**Calibration, anchored to as-built design HMB (nothing fabricated):**

| symbol | value | basis |
|---|---|---|
| $L_0$ | 3.072961 | live reactor-feed NH3/CO2 molar at design steady state |
| $W_0$ | 0.398241 | live reactor-feed H2O/CO2 molar at the design seed |
| $T_0$ | 183.0 °C | `REACT_OVERFLOW_T_C` |
| $X_{\text{des}}$ | 0.543 | $\xi_{\text{urea}} / \mathrm{CO_2}_{\text{feed}} = 1302.27/2397.7$, CO2 per pass |
| $a$ | 3.6180 | NH3-excess saturation coefficient — **frozen**, sets the N/C slope |
| $b$ | 0.85 | water-penalty strength, calibrated up from 0.60 for an aggressive Stamicarbon H/C penalty |
| $X_\infty$ | 0.9140 | **solved**, $= X_{\text{des}} / (f_L(L_0) f_W(W_0))$, so $f_W$ has the headroom a stronger $b$ needs |
| $k$ | 0.0015 1/°C² | parabolic T-penalty curvature |

**Guard 1** — the $(T_0 - T_{\text{opt}})^2$ offset pins $f_T(T_0) = 1.0$ for *any* $T_{\text{opt}}$,
so the design HMB is bit-exact (conversion factor $= 1.000000$ at design) and the downstream
stripper initialisation cannot drift.

**Guard 2** — the hard re-clamp $X = \min(X_\infty f_L f_W f_T, X_\infty)$ honours the thermodynamic
ceiling even where the parabola peak pushes $f_T > 1$ near $T_{\text{opt}}$. This closes the old
unbounded-Arrhenius hole ($X > X_\infty \Rightarrow$ conversion factor $> 1.0 \Rightarrow$ phantom
conversion).

**Over-temperature behaviour** (what a trainee must be able to cause): at the $(L=1000, W=0)$ corner
conversion holds ~91.40 % to ~207 °C, then falls to ~30 % by 225 °C and collapses past 250 °C — a
noticeable drop is already visible by 210 °C. **Equilibrium reversal**, which a bare Arrhenius form
cannot produce.

**What the engine actually consumes:** the *dimensionless* ratio $X(L,W,T)/X(L_0,W_0,T_0)$, which is
exactly 1.000000 at design by construction (Rule 1).

**Known open item:** the settled attractor drifts off the seed — see **handoff B-3**.

## IV.2 322E001 HP stripper — Inoue–Otsuka, anchored extent

Carbamate decomposition driven by CO2 stripping gas. The extent stays **anchored** at design and
the rate law supplies only its response to steam temperature, CO2 rate and liquor loading — same
Rule-1 construction as the reactor.

## IV.3 328C003 hydrolyser — urea hydrolysis

$$
\mathrm{NH_2CONH_2 + H_2O \rightarrow 2\,NH_3 + CO_2}, \qquad k(T) \ \ [\mathrm{m^3\,kmol^{-1}\,h^{-1}}]
$$

second-order, Arrhenius in $T$, with conversion $x$ solved on the residence time of the 200 °C
MP-steam-heated column. *Process utility:* this is the unit that decides the urea content of the
plant's effluent water — the environmental constraint the trainee is being taught to hold.

## IV.4 Biuret formation

$$
\mathrm{2\,NH_2CONH_2 \rightarrow NH_2CONHCONH_2 + NH_3}
$$

Extent $\xi_{\text{biu}}$ tracked per stage as a function of melt temperature and residence time.
*Process utility:* biuret is the product-quality spec that an over-hot evaporator violates. Without
it, a trainee can run the evaporators as hot as they like with no penalty.

---

# Part V — Hydraulics

## V.1 Control valves — IEC 60534-2-1 / ISA-75.01.01 `[V1: hydraulics.py]` → `[ureasim/control/valve.py]`

**What this replaced:** no valve in the engine had a $C_v$. Every flow was
$\text{design} \times (\text{stroke}/\text{stroke}_{\text{des}})$, sometimes
$\times\sqrt{\Delta P/\Delta P_{\text{des}}}$. Three things were wrong: the installed characteristic
was linear whatever the trim, density was absent (it cancels only if constant — which it is not
across 20–99 % urea), and the flow loops carried no $\Delta P$ term at all, so a downstream pressure
change could not move them.

**Incompressible (liquid):**

$$
Q = C_v\, F_p \sqrt{\frac{\Delta P}{G_f}}, \qquad \Delta P_{\text{eff}} = \min\!\big(\Delta P,\; F_L^2 (P_1 - F_F P_v)\big)
$$

**Compressible (gas/vapour), with the expansion factor and the hard choke:**

$$
W = C_v\, N\, Y \sqrt{x\, P_1 \rho_1}, \qquad
Y = 1 - \frac{x}{3 F_\gamma x_T}, \qquad
x = \min\!\left(\frac{\Delta P}{P_1},\; F_\gamma x_T\right)
$$

A choked valve passes a flow that is a function of **upstream conditions only**. Under the old
$\sqrt{\Delta P}$ law, flow kept climbing as downstream pressure fell, *without limit* — and four of
the eight steam-header valves are choked **at their own design point** (HV-329601 vents 9 bar a to
atmosphere; PV-329207A vents 5.01; PV-329207C and HV-329602 both drop 25 → 5.01, all above the
critical $F_\gamma x_T = 0.696$). HV-322604 lets vapour down 140.7 → 4 bar a, a pressure ratio of
0.028 — deeply choked.

**On $C_v$ provenance — read before adding a site.** `References/Datasheets` holds vessel, exchanger
and pump datasheets. It contains **no control-valve datasheets**, so there is no vendor $C_v$ or
$F_L$ anywhere in this repository, and claiming one would be inventing data. `cv_from_design_liquid`
/ `cv_from_design_gas` therefore **back-solve** $C_{v,\max}$ from the licensor's own design duty —
the PFD flow, the design stroke and the design pressures on both sides. That is standard OTS
practice and it is what keeps the boot pin bit-exact: at design stroke and design $\Delta P$ the law
returns the design flow by construction.

**What the back-solve does not give** is the installed characteristic. That is a modelling choice,
stated per site, not hidden: **equal-percentage** for throttling service (what these loops are tuned
around), **linear** for on–off and vent duty. Everything else — the $\Delta P$ term, the density
term, the choke limit, the expansion factor — is first-principles once $C_v$ is fixed, and those are
exactly the terms the frozen form was missing.

## V.2 Vapour-space pressure — real capacitance

**What this replaced:** every vessel pressure was $dP/dt = K(\dot m_{\text{gen}} - \dot m_{\text{out}})$
with a single copy-pasted $K = 0.02$ bar/(kg/s) shared by **nine vessels** of wildly different
volume, temperature and vapour molecular weight — a 0.46 bar a vacuum separator and a 16.8 bar a
hydrolyser on the same coefficient. 323F004 was worse: its pressure was an *algebraic setpoint*
(design $+\,0.45$ bar per unit relative vapour excess) that the state chased through an arbitrary
lag — i.e. **pressure followed flow, when physically flow follows pressure**.

**The real coefficient**, from each vessel's own geometry and live state:

$$
\frac{dP}{dt} \;=\; \frac{R T}{V_v \overline{M}}\big(\dot m_{\text{in}} - \dot m_{\text{out}}\big)
$$

At one vessel the shared capacitance was wrong by **4.69×**.

## V.3 Rotating machinery `[V1: machines.py]` → `[ureasim/control/machines.py]`

### 320K002 CO2 compressor — polytropic map + pressure node

**What this replaced:** no map at all. Discharge pressure was the algebraic assertion
$P_{\text{line}} = \min(P_{\text{syn}} + \Delta P_{\text{des}},\, P_{\text{ceiling}})$ — "the
compressor always delivers exactly the design differential until it cannot." That has **no flow
argument**, so the machine could not be off its curve, could not surge, could not stonewall, and had
no speed.

The split to the HP loop versus the vent was then a normalised conductance ratio
$f_{\text{HP}} = g_{\text{HP}}/(g_{\text{HP}} + g_{\text{vent}})$, $g = \sqrt{\Delta P}$, which
**forces** the branch flows to sum to the raw feed by construction. A real line does not work that
way: the branches meet at a **node**, the node has **one** pressure, and that pressure is whatever
makes the machine's delivery equal what the branches can pass. The ratio form cannot represent a
wide-open vent while the loop is also drawing hard, and cannot let the node pressure fall below the
loop pressure and shut the check valve on its own.

**The model:** polytropic head/flow characteristic in fan-law-reduced coordinates,

$$
\frac{H_p}{N^2} = f\!\left(\frac{Q}{N}\right), \qquad
H_p = \frac{Z R T_1}{M}\cdot\frac{n}{n-1}\left[\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(n-1)/n} - 1\right]
$$

with surge and stonewall limits, and a **node pressure solved so the mass balance closes**.

### 321P002 A/B — triplex reciprocating NH3 pumps

Positive displacement: $D = 140$ mm, $L = 205$ mm, 3 plungers, $\eta_v = 0.95$, $\eta_m = 0.915$.

$$
V_{\text{swept/rev}} = \frac{\pi}{4} D^2 L\, n_{\text{plgr}}, \qquad
Q\,[\mathrm{m^3/h}] = N\,[\text{rpm}] \cdot V_{\text{swept/rev}} \cdot \eta_v \cdot 60
$$

Check: $N = 124$ rpm → 66.91 m³/h (datasheet 67.1); $N = 152$ rpm → 82.02 m³/h (datasheet 82).

**Speed control** is a VOITH torque-converter scoop. The controlled and displayed process variable is
the **torque-converter valve opening (%)**, not rpm: opening $0..100\,\% \rightarrow N = (\text{opening}/100)\,N_{\text{rated}}$.
SIC PV = actual opening %, MV/OP = commanded opening %. Pump rpm is derived and shown separately on
the pump tile. *This distinction is a UI-parity requirement, not a detail.*

## V.4 322F001 HP ejector — liquid-liquid constant-area jet pump `[V1: jet_pump.py]`

322F001 is a **liquid-liquid** jet ejector: HP liquid ammonia from the 321P002 triplex pumps drives
a nozzle, entrains the 322E003 carbamate overflow, mixes in a constant-area throat and recovers
pressure in a diffuser.

**Why not the compressible-ejector module:** a compressible double-choking gas ejector model brings
Mach numbers, isentropic area ratios and normal shocks — **none of which applies**. There is no
sonic condition in a liquid, so the machine has no choked branch to sit on, and its entrainment does
not rise on any motive/suction ratio below choking.

**What this replaced:**

$$
\text{capacity} = \dot m_{\text{suc,des}}\, \phi_m\, \phi_{\text{sp}}\, f_{\text{stall}}, \qquad
f_{\text{stall}} = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\frac{\phi_m - 0.20}{0.35 - 0.20}, 0, 1\right)^2
$$

Every part of that is a curve fitted to the desired behaviour rather than a statement about the
machine: entrainment ratio asserted constant across the healthy band, collapse on a motive fault a
polynomial with three fitted constants and no physical meaning, and the spindle acting on the
**answer** instead of on the **nozzle area**.

**Why the first constant-area attempt was bistable, and what fixes it.** The incompressible attempt
produced a discharge pressure whose $\dot m_s^2$ coefficient was

$$
\frac{1}{\rho_s A_s A_m} - \frac{0.625}{\rho_m A_m^2}
$$

which is **net positive** for any sensible area ratio — so recovered pressure eventually *rises*
with entrainment, the closure has two roots, and the characteristic degenerates to a step.

The missing term is the **suction-inlet acceleration**. The entrained stream does not arrive at the
throat entry plane at rest; it has been accelerated from the suction line to $V_s = \dot m_s/(\rho_s A_s)$,
costing a velocity head

$$
-\,(1 + K_{\text{en}})\,\frac{\dot m_s^2}{2 \rho_s A_s^2}
$$

which enters with $1/A_s^2$ where the cross term enters with $1/(A_s A_m)$. Since $A_s < A_m$ the
missing term is the **larger** of the two, and restoring it flips the sign of the group. This is not
a tuning: with the term in place the coefficient is provably non-positive for **every** area ratio,
so the characteristic is monotone and single-valued.

The spindle acts on the **nozzle area**, where a spindle physically acts.

## V.5 HV-322604 — real-gas isenthalpic letdown `[V1: real_gas.py]`

HV-322604 lets 322E003 off-gas down from the synthesis loop (140.7 bar a) to the LP absorber 322C001
(4.0 bar a).

**What this replaced:** a constant Joule–Thomson coefficient,
$T_{\text{out}} = T_{\text{in}} - 0.55\ \mathrm{^\circ C/bar} \cdot \Delta P \Rightarrow 114 - 0.55(136.7) = 38.8\ \mathrm{^\circ C}$
— a figure typical of an NH3/CO2-rich gas. **PFD stream 204 is not that gas**: it is 68.8 mol% N2,
11.4 % O2, 5.9 % CH4, 3.1 % H2 and only 8.3 % NH3 / 2.2 % CO2. A constant coefficient cannot follow
either the composition or the inlet state.

**A letdown valve is isenthalpic:**

$$
h_{\text{ig}}(T_{\text{out}}) + h_{\text{res}}(T_{\text{out}}, P_{\text{out}}) = h_{\text{ig}}(T_{\text{in}}) + h_{\text{res}}(T_{\text{in}}, P_{\text{in}})
$$

with $h_{\text{ig}}$ from the H0 datum (NIST-JANAF gas $C_p$ — the same datum every stream enthalpy
is published on) and the SRK residual enthalpy:

$$
h_{\text{res}} = RT(Z-1) + \frac{T\,\mathrm{d}a_m/\mathrm{d}T - a_m}{b_m}\ln\!\frac{Z + B}{Z}
$$

**Result:** 94.8 °C at the 322C001 inlet — a mean coefficient of **0.14 K/bar**, a quarter of the
constant, which is what a gas that is mostly nitrogen does. No plant instrument sits downstream of
HV-322604, so this is a first-principles result with no anchor available.

**Scope:** single-phase gas. At the design outlet the NH3 and water partial pressures (0.33 and 0.01
bar) are far from saturation, so no liquid forms; `condensing` flags an outlet where water *would*,
because this routine does not do the two-phase flash that state would need.

## V.6 Line transport — plug flow with flow-dependent delay

$$
t_d = \frac{m_{\text{line}}}{\dot m}, \qquad \text{closed packets advanced FIFO}
$$

*Process utility:* a composition or temperature excursion arrives downstream **later** and
**smeared**, at a delay that *shortens when flow rises*. A fixed lag cannot represent a plant at
turndown, and zero lag teaches a trainee that the plant responds instantly — the single most
damaging thing a simulator can teach.

---

# Part VI — Heat transfer and separation

## VI.1 Exchanger duty

$$
Q = U A\, \Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}}, \qquad
\Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)} \quad\text{(counter-current)}
$$

with $UA$ pinned at design from the PFD duty and the design terminal temperatures, so the design
duty is reproduced by construction (Rule 1).

## VI.2 322C001 LP absorber — rate-based, two packed beds `[V1: packed_absorber.py]`

**Geometry** (sources: UD-AU-322-EC-0007 column datasheet; UD-AU-322-DZ-0007-001 rev 02 as-built
arrangement; UD-AU-322-DZ-0008-001 Rauschert packing datasheet):

* lower bed 1500 mm in the ID 922 section, washed through sprayer N4 by stream 755 (322P002 /
  322E006) and by the CPL leaving the bed above;
* upper bed 1000 mm in the ID 576 section, washed through sprayer N5 by CPL (stream 954);
* packing 25 mm metal Pall rings, Raflux 25-10: $a = 250\ \mathrm{m^2/m^3}$, void 0.95.

**Each bed, each volatile species — counter-current gas-film balance on a straight equilibrium line
(Colburn):**

$$
\frac{y_{\text{out}} - y^*_{\text{in}}}{y_{\text{in}} - y^*_{\text{in}}} = \frac{1 - \lambda}{\exp[\mathrm{NTU}(1-\lambda)] - \lambda}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{mG}{L}
$$

**Transfer units — Onda, Takeuchi & Okumoto (1968):**

$$
\mathrm{NTU} = c_i\,\frac{k_G a_w P Z}{G_m}
$$
$$
\frac{a_w}{a} = 1 - \exp\!\left[-1.45\left(\frac{\sigma_c}{\sigma}\right)^{0.75}\!\mathrm{Re}_L^{0.1}\,\mathrm{Fr}_L^{-0.05}\,\mathrm{We}_L^{0.2}\right]
$$
$$
k_G = 5.23\,\frac{a D_G}{RT}\,\mathrm{Re}_G^{0.7}\,\mathrm{Sc}_G^{1/3}\,(a d_p)^{-2}
$$

**Lower bed:** $y^*_{\text{in}}$ is the NH3/CO2 partial pressure over stream 755 at the live liquor
temperature, and the slope $m = \mathrm{d}p_{\mathrm{NH_3}}/\mathrm{d}x$ over the **live** column
liquor. Both come from the Extended UNIQUAC speciation times the Rumpf–Maurer Henry constant — so
**a liquor that has loaded up or warmed up takes less**, which is the behaviour the trainee must see.

**Upper bed:** CPL enters clean ($y^*_{\text{in}} = 0$). NH3 loads it along its Henry line, and the
bed warms by its own heat of absorption — computed as the *temperature slope of the same speciated
back-pressure*, so CO2 is charged its **carbamate** heat and not its physical solution heat. CO2
reacts with that NH3 ($\lambda = 0$).

**The one number the sources do not supply** is $c_i$. Onda quotes $k_G$ to about ±30 %, so $c_i$ is
solved at the boot pin to make the design uptake exactly the PFD 204 → 797 split: **0.80 for NH3,
0.83 for CO2**. Water is not a transfer-unit species — the vent leaves the CPL wash saturated,
$y_w = a_w\, p^{\text{sat}}(T_{\text{top}})/P$, with $a_w = 0.88$ solved the same way against PFD
797's 2.28 mol%.

## VI.3 Vacuum surface condensers — saturated vent `[V1: vacuum_condenser.py]`

**What this replaced — three stand-ins for one physical fact:**

* gas outlet temperature was the design outlet plus whatever the inlet moved (a **frozen approach**),
  so cooling water could not change it;
* duty became condensate through **one** design "effective enthalpy" per exchanger, so an NH3-rich
  and a water-rich vapour condensed at the same kJ/kg;
* non-condensables derated $UA$ by a linear ratio, and the two pressure loops that actually set
  PT-324201 and PT-324204 **did not use the node at all** — they subtracted the *design* condensate
  as a constant, so the condenser could not respond to its own shell pressure.

**The physics.** Every PFD vent row off these condensers sits at water saturation at its own
temperature and pressure — stream 706 is 29.4 mol% H2O at 45 °C / 0.33 bar a ($p_{H_2O}$ 0.097
against $p^{\text{sat}}$ 0.096); 712 is 57.9 % at 40 °C / 0.131 (0.076 vs 0.074); 722 is 15.2 % at
55 °C / 1.0 (0.152 vs 0.157). That is what a surface condenser *does*: the gas leaving the cold end
is the inert gas plus whatever vapour it can hold at that end's temperature and the shell pressure.

$$
y_c(T_v, P) = Y_{\text{des}}\,\frac{P_{\text{des}}}{P}\cdot\frac{p^{\text{sat}}_w(T_v)}{p^{\text{sat}}_w(T_{v,\text{des}})}, \qquad
\dot n_{\text{vent},c} = \dot n_{\text{inert}}\,\frac{y_c}{1 - y_c}
$$

and the vent grows **without bound** — until it is the whole inlet — as shell pressure falls toward
the vapour pressure at the cold end. That is the vacuum-break mechanism, emergent rather than
scripted.

**NH3 and CO2 carry their own partial pressures** (they used to ride water's saturation line with a
fixed split, because the engine's activity grid stops at 80 °C and these cold ends are 40–55 °C; the
absorber's `back_pressure` covers 10–100 °C):

$$
p_w = Y_{\text{des}} s_w P_{\text{des}}\frac{p^{\text{sat}}_w(T_v)}{p^{\text{sat}}_w(T_{v,\text{des}})}, \qquad
p_k = Y_{\text{des}} s_k P_{\text{des}}\frac{p^*_k(w_{\text{cond}}, T_v)}{p^*_k(w_{\text{cond,des}}, T_{v,\text{des}})}
$$
$$
y_c = \frac{p_w + p_{\mathrm{NH_3}} + p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{P}, \qquad
\dot n_{\text{vent},k} = \dot n_{\text{inert}}\frac{y_c}{1-y_c}\cdot\frac{p_k}{\sum p}
$$

Unanchored, the speciation over PFD condensate 719 at 45 °C gives $p_{\mathrm{NH_3}} = 0.054$ and
$p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 0.0085$ bar against PFD 706's 0.059 and 0.013. An ammonia-rich inlet then raises
$p_{\mathrm{NH_3}}$ **more than in proportion**, because less of it is bound to CO2.

**The cold-end temperature is solved, not assigned:**

$$
Q_{\text{bal}}(T_v) = H_{\text{gas}}(\text{inlet}, T_{\text{in}}) - H_{\text{gas}}(\text{vent}, T_v) - H_{\text{liq}}(\text{condensate}, T_v) \;=\; UA\,\Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}}(T_v)
$$

## VI.4 Kremser / stage efficiency

$$
S = \frac{mV}{L}, \qquad \frac{x_{\text{in}} - x_{\text{out}}}{x_{\text{in}} - x^*} = \frac{S^{N}-S}{S^{N}-1}
$$

used where a column is represented by theoretical stages rather than by transfer units.

## VI.5 Souders–Brown disengagement

$$
v_{\max} = K\sqrt{\frac{\rho_L - \rho_V}{\rho_V}}
$$

*Process utility:* sets where a separator begins to carry liquid over. The consequence of exceeding
it is entrainment into the overhead — not an alarm, a **mass flow**.

---

# Part VII — Unit-operation balances, section by section

Every unit obeys the MESH set:

$$
\textbf{M:}\ \sum_{\text{in}} F_j - \sum_{\text{out}} F_j = \frac{\mathrm{d}M}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$
$$
\textbf{C:}\ \sum_{\text{in}} F_j x_{i,j} - \sum_{\text{out}} F_j x_{i,j} + r_i V = \frac{\mathrm{d}(M x_i)}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$
$$
\textbf{E:}\ \sum_{\text{in}} F_j H_j - \sum_{\text{out}} F_j H_j + Q - W = \frac{\mathrm{d}(M h)}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$
$$
\textbf{S:}\ y_i = K_i x_i, \qquad \sum_i x_i = 1, \qquad \sum_i y_i = 1
$$

## VII.1 Unit 321 — NH3 pumping station

* **321D003 feed drum** — ID 0.97 m, H 1.4 m (cyl) ⇒ $V = 1.0345\ \mathrm{m^3}$.
  Mass balance $\mathrm{d}m/\mathrm{d}t = F_{\text{in,BL}} - F_{\text{pump,total}}$.
* **321P002 A/B** — triplex displacement law, §V.3.
* **Ratio block** — $\mathrm{SP}_{\mathrm{NH_3\ flow}} = r_{\mathrm{SP}} \cdot F_{\mathrm{CO_2}}$.
  In CAS the SIC opening SP is derived from the required NH3 flow split across active pumps, with a
  per-pump N/C operator bias.

## VII.2 Unit 322 — HP synthesis loop

320K002 → CO2 feed node → 322E001 stripper → 322E002 HPCC → 322R001 reactor → 322E003 HP scrubber
→ HV-322604 purge → 322C001; with 322F001 recirculating carbamate on HP liquid ammonia.

* **PT-329201 synthesis-loop pressure** — a capacitive node (§V.2), not an assignment.
* **322E002 HPCC** — tube-side condensation raising LP steam on the shell; bubble pressure
  $P_{\text{bub}}(T, L, W)$ closes the tube side.
* **322E003 HP scrubber** — reactor off-gas washed by weak carbamate from 323P001 A/B, cooled by CCW;
  sump inventory ODE; LT-329501 carries a **two-phase hydrodynamic swell** overlay so the DP
  transmitter reads what a DP transmitter reads, not the true level.

## VII.3 Unit 323 — LP recirculation, four stages

| stage | equipment | design state | mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 323C003 rectifying column + 323E002 heater | 4.1 bar a, 135 °C | two-path pressure (§VII.3.1) |
| 2 | 323F004 flash tank | 1.13 bar a, 106 °C | adiabatic letdown |
| 3 | 323F010 pre-evaporator + 323E010 | 0.46 bar a, 99 °C | vacuum flash |
| 4 | 323D002 urea solution tank | atmospheric, two compartments | buffer + communicating compartments |

Plus the condensing side: 323E003/323D001 LPCC (74 °C, tempered water) and 323E011/323D011 LP
carbamate condenser (45 °C).

### VII.3.1 PT-323201 — two independent gas-load paths

PT-323201 is charged by two physically distinct carbamate-gas sources, tabulated separately by the
PFD at 4.1 bar a:

* **stream 301** — prompt flash gas released across LV-322501 as the 144 bar stripper bottoms let
  down to 4.1 bar a (5064.7 m³/h, 119 °C, MW 26.39), entering above the packed bed with the 311
  reflux;
* **stream 302** — gas evolved in the 323E002 rectifying heater and returned **below** the bed
  (2875.7 m³/h, 135 °C, MW 21.14).

Keeping them separate gives each source its own coupling chain — opening LV-322501 ⇒ more flash gas
⇒ higher column pressure; more 323E002 duty ⇒ more evolved gas ⇒ higher column pressure — and
neither term is inferred from the other.

**Why stream 305 is not used as an inlet:** 305 (7677.1 m³/h) is the column **outlet**.
301 + 302 = 7940.4 m³/h enter, and 263.3 m³/h (3.3 %) condense on the bed where the 135 °C heater gas
meets the 119 °C reflux. Driving an inlet term with 305 would make the total feed back on itself.

**Design identity:** both ratios 1.0 against a 3.2 bar a downstream node returns exactly 4.1 bar a,
the PFD anchor.

**Open calibration item:** the field-trend gain on the LV-322501 signal — see **handoff B-4**.

## VII.4 Unit 328 — desorption and hydrolysis, nine stages

323C005 vent scrub → 328V001 → 328D003 (active bays I/II + communicating accumulation bay III) →
328E007 feed/effluent interchanger → 328C002 Desorber-I (bottoms 139 °C, floats PIC-328202) →
328C003 hydrolyser (200 °C, MP steam 911) → 328C004 Desorber-II (143 °C, LP steam 931, FFIC) →
328D001 Desorber-I reflux drum (61 °C, 328E004) → 322C001 LP absorber → 323E003/323D001 LPCC →
323E011/323D011.

**Communicating compartments** (328D003 bays, 323D002 compartments) redistribute mass and
temperature across a shared weir:

$$
\text{redistribute}(m_k, T_k, m_{k,\text{full}}) \;\rightarrow\; \text{common level, mixing-weighted } T
$$

*Process utility:* a bay that fills does not simply stop — it spills into its neighbour, and the
neighbour's temperature moves. That is what makes a level upset in 328 propagate.

## VII.5 Unit 324 — evaporation and finishing

* **Stage 1** — 324E001 + separator 324F001, 0.33 bar a, 130 °C.
* **Stage 2** — 324E003 + separator 324F003, 0.131 bar a, 140 °C.
* **Vacuum train** — four surface condensers (§VI.3) plus steam-jet ejectors and the barometric leg.
* **UF85 injection** — FFIC-335406 ratio station → FIC-335405 flow.

Both evaporator stages use the neutral-UNIQUAC domain for the water activity, and keep an **anchored
vapour vector** for the NH3/CO2 split — see **handoff B-1**.

### VII.5.1 Melt-temperature integration — why a draining evaporator killed the engine

A draining vessel makes $\mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}t$ stiff: as $M \rightarrow 0$ the coefficient
$1/(M c_p)$ blows up, and an explicit Euler step on

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\dot m_{\text{in}} c_p (T_{\text{in}} - T) + Q}{M c_p}
$$

diverges. **The fix is a better integration scheme, not a limiter.** Semi-implicit (backward on the
$T$ term):

$$
T^{n+1} = \frac{T^n + \dfrac{\Delta t}{M c_p}\big(\dot m_{\text{in}} c_p T_{\text{in}} + Q\big)}{1 + \dfrac{\Delta t\, \dot m_{\text{in}}}{M}}
$$

which is unconditionally stable and reduces to the explicit form as $\Delta t \rightarrow 0$. The same
construct sat at **eleven more integrators** and was swept.

A limiter would have hidden the divergence and made the evaporator unable to cool at its true rate;
the scheme change fixes the cause.

## VII.6 Unit 329 — steam network `[V1: steam_system.py]`

**Four pressure levels**, lumped-capacitance headers integrated by explicit Euler at the host $\Delta t$:

| level | pressure | vessel | supply |
|---|---|---|---|
| BL supply | 25.0 bar a | — (held boundary) | stream 901 from 320E006 |
| HP saturator | 19.7 bar a | 329D005 | 902 in → HP stripper 322E001 shell |
| MP drum | 9.0 bar a | 329D009 | 903 in → 9-bar header + PV-329205B let-down |
| LP drums | 4.4 bar a | 322D001 A/B | HPCC steam-raising + 9→4 let-down + 963 in |

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\sum \dot m_{\text{in}} - \sum \dot m_{\text{out}}}{C}, \qquad C\ \ [(\mathrm{kg/s})/\mathrm{bar}]
$$

**Desuperheating water on a let-down** (attemperator to saturated downstream):

$$
\dot m_{\text{water}} = \dot m_{\text{ld}}\,\frac{h_{g,\text{up}} - h_{g,\text{dn}}}{h_{g,\text{dn}} - h_w}
$$

**Valve flows are compressible** (§V.1) — the four choked valves are the reason.

**Bit-exact design anchor:** the plant H&MB couples to this module through only two saturation
temperatures — $T_{\text{sat}}(P_{\mathrm{MP}})$ to the HP-stripper reboiler and
$T_{\text{sat}}(P_{\mathrm{LP}})$ to the HPCC shell — so $P_{\mathrm{MP}}$ and $P_{\mathrm{LP}}$ are
held at their design saturation pressures (19.7 / 4.4 bar a) by the HP supply seed.

### VII.6.1 Steam-chest pressure — solved, not assigned

$$
\text{residual}(P_{\text{chest}}) = \dot m_{\text{valve}}(P_{\text{hdr}} \rightarrow P_{\text{chest}})\,\lambda(P_{\text{chest}}) - UA\,\big(T_{\text{sat}}(P_{\text{chest}}) - T_{\text{process}}\big) = 0
$$

solved for $P_{\text{chest}}$ each tick. *Process utility:* a steam-heated shell whose chest pressure
is assigned cannot respond to a fouled tube bundle or a throttled supply valve. Solving the residual
makes both visible to the trainee.

# Part VIII — Control and interlock mathematics

> **As built, see Part XV.** This part states the control mathematics as the rewrite planned it. Part XV records what was actually ported, which differs in one structural way worth knowing before reading on: V1 has **two** I-PD implementations and uses both, so the rewrite has two as well. It also documents the $T_d = -1$ sentinel, the two $F_F$ conventions in the liquid valve law, and the four trip shapes including 21.4, which is not listed in §VIII.4 below.

## VIII.1 PID — velocity I-PD form `[V1: controllers.py]` → `[ureasim/control/controller.py]`

$$
\Delta u_k = K_c\Big[-(PV_k - PV_{k-1}) + \frac{\Delta t}{T_i}(SP_k - PV_k) - T_d\,\frac{PV_k - 2PV_{k-1} + PV_{k-2}}{\Delta t}\Big]
$$

then, in order:

$$
\Delta u_k \leftarrow \operatorname{clamp}(\sigma \Delta u_k,\ -\text{rate}\cdot\Delta t,\ +\text{rate}\cdot\Delta t) \quad\text{(slew limit)}
$$
$$
u_k \leftarrow \operatorname{clamp}(u_{k-1} + \Delta u_k,\ u_{lo},\ u_{hi}) \quad\text{(output clamp / anti-windup)}
$$

$\sigma = +1$ reverse acting, $-1$ direct acting; $K_c > 0$ always.

**Why I-PD and not textbook PID:** proportional and derivative act on **PV**, not on error, so a
setpoint step does not kick the valve. On a plant where SP changes are an operator action being
trained, derivative kick on every SP entry is both unphysical and pedagogically wrong. The velocity
form gives bumpless MAN↔AUTO↔CAS transfer for free, because the controller carries $u_{k-1}$ rather
than an integral accumulator that must be back-calculated.

Modes: **MAN** (operator sets OP directly), **AUTO** (local SP + PID), **CAS** (SP from a master),
**OOS**.

## VIII.2 Ratio and cascade

$$
SP_{\text{slave}} = r_{SP}\cdot PV_{\text{wild}} \quad (+\ \text{operator bias})
$$

## VIII.3 First-order lag and FOPTD

$$
\tau\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} + y = u(t - t_d) \quad\Rightarrow\quad
y_{k+1} = y_k + \frac{\Delta t}{\tau}\big(u_{\text{delayed}} - y_k\big)
$$

Used for instrument dynamics and display lags, so an indicator does not step when the underlying
state steps.

## VIII.4 Interlocks

Stateful latching trips: TRIP_21_2, TRIP_21_8, TRIP_21_10, Trip 22.1 (LP absorber 322C001
over-temperature steam flood), Trip 22.2 (synthesis high-high pressure → ESD). Latched, with an
explicit operator reset — **not** a comparison evaluated fresh each tick, because a trip that
un-trips itself teaches the wrong lesson.

## VIII.5 Crystallisation flow derate

$$
f_{\text{flow}}(T) = \text{smooth ramp over } [T_{\text{cryst}},\ T_{\text{cryst}} + \Delta T_{\text{mush}}], \quad \Delta T_{\text{mush}} = 5\ \mathrm{K}
$$

*Process utility:* a carbamate line does not block instantly at the solubility temperature — it
thickens over a few kelvin. A step would chatter; the ramp makes the line's restriction
proportional to how far below the solubility curve it has fallen.

# Part IX — Deviation-consequence physics

`[V1: consequence.py]` → `[ureasim/units/consequence/]`

## IX.1 Why this layer exists at all

Before it, every deviation scenario was wired into the engine at the **one tag it had been written
up against**, with its own hand-picked constant:

| scenario | old code |
|---|---|
| 322E001 seal loss | $25000 \cdot (\theta/\theta_{\text{des}})\sqrt{\Delta P/\Delta P_{\text{des}}}$ |
| 323C003 seal loss | $5000 \cdot (\theta/\theta_{\text{des}})$ |
| 323F004 seal loss | $5000 \cdot (\theta/\theta_{\text{des}})$ |
| 323F004 overfill | $(\text{level} - 100)\cdot 100$ — **identically zero**, level is clamped to 100 |
| 328D001 low level | $\dot m = 0$ at $M \le 1.5$ kg — a **cliff**, not a pump curve |
| 324F003 low level | $P := 1.013$ bar a — a **state override**, cannot recover |

Three things are wrong with that, and this layer fixes all three.

1. **Unequal consequences for equal causes.** Losing the liquid seal on 323C003 and on 328C004 is
   the *same event* — a drain nozzle uncovers and the vessel's gas inventory escapes through a valve
   sized for liquid. One produced 5000 kg/h of gas and the other produced nothing, because nobody had
   written that scenario down yet. **A trainee who learns the plant on a model like that learns the
   model's authoring history, not the plant.**
2. **Unphysical magnitudes.** 25000 and 5000 kg/h are not measurements; they are numbers that made a
   demo look right. The mass a valve passes when its seal breaks is not a free parameter — the
   valve's $C_v$ is fixed by its *liquid* design duty, and gas flow through that same coefficient
   follows IEC 60534 with a real expansion factor and a real choke point. *(Sanity check: the derived
   LV-322501 rate lands at ~30 t/h against the 25 t/h picked by hand — so the hand number was the
   right order. It simply could not be transferred to any other valve, which is the entire problem.)*
3. **Discontinuities and state overrides.** See Rule 3.

## IX.2 Loss of liquid seal — gas blow-through

The drain valve's own $C_v$, back-solved from its liquid design duty, evaluated on the **gas**
compressible law when the nozzle uncovers:

$$
\dot m_{\text{gas}} = C_v\,N\,Y\sqrt{x P_1 \rho_{1,\text{gas}}}, \qquad x = \min(\Delta P/P_1,\ F_\gamma x_T)
$$

Continuous in level through the nozzle-uncovering fraction, so it starts, grows and stops smoothly.

## IX.3 Liquid carry-over — Souders–Brown

Excess velocity over $v_{\max}$ (§VI.5) becomes an **entrained mass flow** into the overhead, which
the downstream balance then has to deal with. Not an alarm.

## IX.4 Pump NPSH — one equation for "level fell" and "temperature rose"

$$
\mathrm{NPSH_a} = \frac{P_{\text{vessel}} - P_v(T)}{\rho g} + h_{\text{static}} - h_{\text{friction}}
$$

Both failure modes are the *same* equation: a falling level cuts $h_{\text{static}}$; a rising
temperature raises $P_v(T)$. Cavitation derates head continuously as $\mathrm{NPSH_a}$ approaches
$\mathrm{NPSH_r}$ — it does not trip at a threshold.

## IX.5 Crystallisation — a solubility curve, not a constant

$$
T_{\text{cryst}} = f(w_{\text{urea}}, w_{\mathrm{NH_3}}, w_{\mathrm{CO_2}})
$$

from the carbamate/urea solubility surface. A constant crystallisation temperature cannot represent
a line that becomes *more* prone to blocking as it is diluted with carbamate — which is the actual
plant behaviour.

## IX.6 Vacuum break — a load, not an assignment

Air in-leak and condenser underperformance enter as a **load** on the vacuum train (§VI.3), which
then finds its own pressure. Pressure is never assigned. The trainee can therefore *recover* the
vacuum by fixing the cause.

## IX.7 Transport lag on every consequence

A consequence arrives at the affected equipment after the line transport delay (§V.6), not
instantly.

# Part X — Numerical methods

| method | where | why |
|---|---|---|
| Explicit Euler | steam headers, most inventories | cheap, stable at 10 Hz for these time constants |
| **Semi-implicit (backward on the decay term)** | all twelve melt/temperature integrators | a draining vessel makes $1/(Mc_p)$ stiff — §VII.5.1 |
| Backward Euler on pressure | vapour-space nodes with fast dynamics | avoids a $\Delta t$ limit set by the smallest vapour space |
| Damped log-space Newton | R1–R5 speciation | keeps molalities positive; converges from a poor guess |
| Bisection | bubble points, flash $\beta$ | bracketing is guaranteed and cheap; robustness beats speed here |
| Newton with converged-neighbour seeding | activity table build | the dilute initial guess fails above $N\approx40$; the *same* solver reaches $N=869$ in five steps when seeded |
| Sequential-modular + tear | flowsheet recycles | matches the plant's directed topology; tears are written at tick end and read at the next tick |
| Rachford–Rice | two-phase flash | standard, well-conditioned in $\beta$ |

**Recycle tearing.** Loops are torn, and the tear variables are written at the **end** of a tick for
the **next** tick to read. This is a deliberate one-tick delay: at 10 Hz it is 0.1 s of artificial
transport on a loop whose real time constants are minutes, and it removes the need for an inner
iteration that would make the frame rate non-deterministic.

**The step is fixed at 0.1 s** (decided 2026-09-27, handoff A-14; `Claude.md` §1 rule 10). Because
every tear carries exactly one step of delay, the step IS the tear delay, and it must not move. V1
steps on the wall clock (`sim_task`: the elapsed time since the last pass, capped at 0.5 s, times
the pacing factor, in sub-steps of at most `STEP_CAP` = 0.25 s), so its transients depend on
machine load. The engine instead pays `elapsed x pacing` in whole 0.1 s steps out of an
accumulator — V1's `DT`, the step of its design pin and of every equivalence test — so SLOW and
FAST run the same steps and an exercise replays bit for bit. The Phase 7 comparison drives V1 at the
same fixed step.

| 347 | PV-329204, PV-329207A / B, PV-329208 and PV-329212 on Valmet's S-Disc table through their sheets' printed points (decision 170) | the chord between the printed points and from the last to wide open (decisions 108, 153) | `data/control_valves_metso` ``S_DISC_RELATIVE_CV``, ``_s_disc``; every unit's ``*_OP_DES_PCT`` through ``design_stroke_pct`` | **`[DECIDED DIVERGENCE]`** 2026-11-06: every printed point and the rated capacity kept, the table's shape between them; design strokes 55.9717 % (PV-329207B, 54.9630 on the chord), 27.2640 % (PV-329208, 27.2232) and 54.6843 % (PV-329212, 54.6805), PV-329204's 44.1 % and PV-329207A's full stroke unchanged; the chord rebuilt through ``_neldisc`` for the test, both ways in `test_decision_170_both_sides`; the nine conventional Neldiscs keep the chord (§CI.1) |

**Rule for this table:** a row moves to `[PORTED]` only when (a) the code is in `ureasim/`, (b) an
equivalence test in `tests/equivalence/` drives both implementations and passes, and (c) the
achieved tolerance is recorded in the row.

A `[PORTED]` row may also carry a **decided divergence**: a place where the rewrite deliberately
does not do what V1 does, because the process engineer decided so on a handoff item. The row
names the divergence, the equivalence test asserts BOTH sides of it — what V1 does and what the
rewrite does instead — and the section the row links to records the decision and its date. The
handoff item is then deleted. Row 36 is the first.

Row 38 is the first `[PORTED]` row proven **wholly by execution of a V1 function**, rather
than by a mixture of executed correlations and transcribed wiring. `tests/equivalence/v1_loader.py`
`lift()` compiles the statements that define a set of V1 names, plus the transitive closure of
everything those statements read, and runs them — which is how a function inside an
unimportable `main.py` can still be driven side by side with its replacement.

`[TRANSCRIBED]` is a weaker state, used for exactly one row. It means the V1 source cannot be
executed in isolation — the trip logic is written inline inside `step_sim` and reads a plant
state that only exists after `main.py` has built a FastAPI application — so the rules are
transcribed into the test and checked by eye against the source. A transcribed row is not a
ported row and is tracked as an open item (handoff A-12) until it can be executed.

**Tolerance achieved on rows 1-8: bit-for-bit (`==`, not `approx`).** The port changed layout
and documentation only — the coefficient tables and the evaluation order are unchanged — so
anything short of exact equality would be a transcription error, and the tests assert exact
equality rather than a tolerance. 412 assertions over the plant's own operating states:
0.131–25 bar a, 40–224 °C, and loadings from the dilute reference to N = 100 mol/kg water at
the 322R001 overflow.

**Phase 1 is complete.** The thermodynamic core is 18 modules, every one under the 600-line
house cap, and the whole of it is proven against V1. Two independent confirmations worth
recording, because they check the *physics* rather than the transcription:

* the rebuilt 1215-node activity table converges at **every** node and reproduces the
  documented PFD validation exactly — 323C003 +6.1 %, 323F004 +15.0 %, 323F010 +1.8 %;
* `k_ratio` returns **exactly 1.0** at its own reference point for every stage tested, which
  is the property the entire HP-loop anchoring rests on (Part 0, Rule 1).

# Part XII — HMI geometry

The presentation layer carries no process equations, but it does carry one piece of
mathematics the drawings depend on. It is recorded here because getting it wrong silently
mis-places every rotated symbol on the plant.

## XII.1 The anisotropic slide mapping

PowerPoint slides are 12 192 000 × 6 858 000 EMU; the HMI stage is 1366 × 720 px. Both are
16:9, but the scale factors are not equal:

$$
s_x = \frac{1366}{12\,192\,000}, \qquad
s_y = \frac{720}{6\,858\,000}, \qquad
\mathrm{SLIDE\_RX} = \frac{s_x}{s_y} = 1.0671875
$$

The render is stretched 6.7 % wider than it is tall relative to the drawing. For an
unrotated box that is irrelevant — the element is sized in stage pixels and lands in the hole
its symbol left. For a **rotated** icon it is not: a pump rotated 90° and then stretched
horizontally is an ellipse.

## XII.2 The transform, and its order

Reproduce the slide's own order — draw at the un-stretched size, rotate, then stretch:

$$
\text{image size} = \left(\frac{w}{\mathrm{SLIDE\_RX}}\right) \times h
$$

$$
T = \underbrace{\mathrm{scale}_x(\mathrm{SLIDE\_RX})}_{\text{applied last}} \cdot
    \mathrm{rotate}(\theta) \cdot
    \underbrace{\mathrm{scale}(\pm 1, \pm 1)}_{\text{applied first}}
$$

Mirror the symbol inside its own box, rotate the box, then undo the stage's squash. Exact for
any $\theta$; at $\theta = 0$ with no mirror it collapses to a plain $w \times h$ box.

**The bug this replaced.** V1 kept a fixed 54×54 / 34×34 default box while the image inside
carried the real size. Because the box is centred but the image is laid out from its
top-left, every icon sat half the size difference off its symbol — the 321-1 pumps by
11 × 6 px and the XVs by 17. The widget box is now the same un-stretched rectangle as the
image, so centring the widget centres the symbol.

Implementation: `ureasim/hmi/widgets/icon_geometry.py`. Gate:
`tests/hmi/test_screen_geometry.py::test_overlay_is_centred_on_its_recorded_point`, which
asserts every one of the 387 elements is centred on its recorded point to within 0.5 px.

## XII.3 The display-unit convention

Every pressure transmitter and controller on these screens shows **gauge** pressure while the
engine works in absolute. The conversion happens once, at the display boundary:

$$
u = \text{BAR A} \;\Rightarrow\; v_{\text{shown}} = v - 1.01325, \quad
u_{\text{shown}} = \text{BARG}
$$

Doing it in the engine would corrupt the physics; doing it per widget would guarantee that
one widget eventually forgets. Implementation: `ureasim/hmi/state_access.to_display_units`.

## XII.4 Indicator box model

An indicator is sized by its **value**, not by the label it replaced, so the box model has to
be exact — two boxes on 324-1b sit 80 px apart:

$$
W = 2b + 2p + w_{\text{value}}
    + [\,g + w_{\text{unit}}\,]
    + [\,g + w_{\text{mode}}\,],
\qquad b = 1,\; p = 4,\; g = 3 \ \text{px}
$$

A Qt layout's size hint carries each child label's own margins plus the layout's spacing,
which inflated this by about 20 px and produced collisions the drawing does not have. The
indicator is therefore painted, not laid out.

# Part XIII — Station transport

The transport carries no process equations, but it carries two rules that decide what a
trainee learns, so they are recorded here rather than left in code comments.

## XIII.1 One refusal: the process's

Until 2026-10-22 a command could be rejected for two different reasons, kept apart so an operator
could tell them apart:

$$
\text{refusal} =
\begin{cases}
\textbf{role} & \text{the server: this role may not issue this command type} \[2pt]
\textbf{process} & \text{the engine: the plant will not accept it}
\end{cases}
$$

**The role refusal is retired by decision 149** (the single-console conversion, Part LXXXIII): the
server checks no role, so the only refusal left is the process's — a latched trip, an interlock, a
closed valve — and its reason is the engine's own. It travels back to the console's status bar with
that reason, so a trainee learns why the plant would not take the action.

V1 had neither: an unknown command reached `handle_cmd`, matched no branch, and was
discarded in silence. A trainee learned that the plant ignored them.

## XIII.2 What the console may do

Until 2026-10-22 the server gated the commands that are not plant equipment behind the instructor
role:

$$
\text{gated}(c) \;=\;
\big[\, c \in \text{INSTRUCTOR\_ONLY} \,\big] \;\lor\;
\big[\, c \text{ ends with } \texttt{\_fault} \,\big]
$$

with an observer commanding nothing and an operator every ungated command. **The role gate is
retired by decision 149**: the single console sends every command the engine takes. The separation
is now the console's layout. The process screens and their faceplates keep exactly what V1's
operator screens exposed — every controller, valve, pump, hand station and ratio block —
because re-classifying a plant control would change what a trainee is being taught, which Part 0's
fidelity rules forbid. The controls that are not plant equipment — malfunction injection and
clearing, reset, simulation pacing, freeze, exercise save and restore, and the battery-limit CO2
demand (`co2_set`, decision 73) — sit in the Instructor menu's panel.

## XIII.3 Snapshot back-pressure

A console that cannot keep up must not be able to consume the engine's memory, and it must
not be shown stale plant data when it recovers:

$$
\text{send}(f) =
\begin{cases}
\text{drop} & q > q_{\max} \
\text{write} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad q_{\max} = 2
$$

where $q$ counts consecutive publishes for which the station's write buffer was still
non-empty. **Snapshots are droppable; commands and acknowledgements are not.** Losing a
frame of a 10 Hz animation costs nothing — the next one carries the current state. Losing
an operator action is not acceptable.

## XIII.4 Why a stale link blanks the screen

A half-open TCP connection reports nothing until it is written to, so a console can sit
"connected" long after the engine has gone. The only reliable evidence is the absence of
snapshots, so a watchdog fires after 5 s without one.

On firing, every indicator returns to `--`. It would be easy to leave the last values on
screen, and it would be wrong: a frozen screen that still looks live is the single most
dangerous thing an operator console can do, and on a training simulator it teaches a
trainee to trust one.
