# Part XIV — The core flowsheet layer

Everything in `ureasim/core` sits between the property packages and the unit operations. It
carries no correlations: it is the plumbing a unit operation is written against. The
relations below are recorded because the *conventions* are load bearing even though the
mathematics is elementary — an argument order, a cap, a limiter's NaN behaviour or a
rounding digit changed here moves a published plant number.

## XIV.1 The stream packet

One sample of a flowing stream, taken at an equipment boundary and treated as indivisible.

$$
\text{packet} \;=\; \bigl(\dot m,\; T,\; c_p,\; \{\dot m_i\}\bigr),
\qquad \dot m \;=\; \sum_i \dot m_i \ \ \text{by construction}
$$

with the three derived views

$$
w_i = \frac{\dot m_i}{\dot m}, \qquad
\dot H_{\text{sens}} = \frac{\dot m\, c_p\, T}{3600} \ \ [\mathrm{kW}]
$$

**Process utility.** The defect this prevents is *property desynchronisation*. Modelled as
three separate signals, a boundary can deliver this tick's flow at last tick's temperature
carrying the tick-before's composition. The inventory still balances, so nothing looks
wrong; only the energy balance quietly stops closing, and a trainee sees a stage respond
before the material that should have caused the response has arrived. Holding the three on
one frozen object makes that unrepresentable.

The constructor **refuses** a stated total that disagrees with the component sum by more
than $\max(10^{-9},\,10^{-9}\max(|\Sigma|,|\dot m|,1))$. A caller whose total comes from a
different expression than its components is how a mass balance stops closing, and it is
caught at the boundary rather than three units downstream.

**Mixing is an energy balance, not an average:**

$$
c_{p,\text{mix}} = \frac{\sum_k \dot m_k c_{p,k}}{\sum_k \dot m_k},
\qquad
T_{\text{mix}} = \frac{\sum_k \dot m_k c_{p,k} T_k}{\sum_k \dot m_k c_{p,k}}
$$

These differ from a flow-weighted mean temperature whenever the streams have different heat
capacities, which at a 328D003 inlet taking four condensates they do.

## XIV.2 Plug-flow transport — the line between two vessels

$$
t_d \;=\; \frac{\rho\, V_{\text{line}}}{\dot m}, \qquad
V_{\text{line}} \;=\; \frac{\pi}{4} D^2 L
$$

**Process utility.** Without it, a property step at one vessel's outlet is consumed by the
next vessel on the same tick — the parcel teleports. And the dead time must *move with
flow*: at 50 % load the real transit time doubles, and a trainee who cuts a feed has to see
the downstream response get **slower**, not merely smaller. A fixed FIFO lag cannot do that.

A route is specified by its design pair $(\dot m_{\text{des}}, t_{d,\text{des}})$, because
that is what the PFD and the layout give. The physically constant quantity follows:

$$
M_{\text{line}} \;=\; \frac{\dot m_{\text{des}}\, t_{d,\text{des}}}{3600},
\qquad
t_d(\dot m) \;=\; \mathrm{clamp}\!\left(\frac{3600\,M_{\text{line}}}{\dot m},\; 0,\; t_{d,\max}\right)
$$

so the route is anchored at design (Rule 1) and responds correctly off design with nothing
fitted anywhere.

**Two transit-time forms are kept, deliberately.** V1 defines `transport_time_s` in both
`hydraulics.py` and `consequence.py`. Same equation, different guards, different caps
(3600 s against 1800 s) and different argument orders. Merging them would silently re-cap
one family of call sites, so `core.transport` ports both under names that say which is
which, and each ported call site keeps the one V1 gave it.

**The FIFO is timestamped, not counted.** The integrator advances in bounded sub-steps whose
size is not fixed; a remainder sub-step is frequently of order $10^{-8}$ s. A buffer sized
as $n = t_d/\Delta t$ would need about $10^{10}$ entries on one of those. Timestamping the
samples and zero-order-holding against a per-sub-step clock removes the dependence on
$\Delta t$ entirely.

**The two seedings are not interchangeable.** A *consequence* line starts empty, because a
leak that has not happened yet must not arrive at $t = 0$. A *process* line starts full of
its first packet, because the 323C003-to-323F004 product line is full of 135 °C liquor at
simulation start; a line that started empty would starve the whole recirculation train for
one dead time on every boot and break the design pin.

**Route inventories, as built.** Bore 187.1 mm, DN 200, from the 323C003 nozzle schedule;
run lengths are layout estimates (handoff A-11).

| route | design carrier (kg/h) | design $t_d$ (s) | line inventory (kg) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 322E001 → 323C003 | 130 482 | 21.81 | 790.5 |
| 323C003 → 323F004 | 105 919 | 15.98 | 470.1 |
| 323F004 → 323F010 | 101 492 | 16.75 | 472.2 |
| 323F010 → 323D002 | 92 749 | 36.85 | 949.4 |
| 323D002 → 324E001 | 92 749 | 49.13 | 1 265.8 |

## XIV.3 Signal conditioning — what an indicator does to a value

An operator does not see the plant, they see the instruments, and the instruments lag.

$$
\text{lag:}\quad y_{k+1} = y_k + a\,(u - y_k), \qquad a = \frac{\Delta t}{\tau + \Delta t}
$$

$$
\text{dead time:}\quad y(t) = u(t - t_d)
\qquad\qquad
\text{FOPTD:}\quad G(s) = \frac{e^{-t_d s}}{\tau s + 1}
$$

The lag is implicit (backward) Euler, unconditionally stable for **any** ratio of $\Delta t$
to $\tau$ — including the crumb sub-steps above, where an explicit form would ring. At
steady state it converges exactly to its input, so the design pin survives.

**These act on published signals only.** A lag applied to a *state* is an invented time
constant, which the agent directives forbid: the dynamics of a vessel come from its
inventory and its duty, not from a filter bolted on afterwards. Separating `core.signal`
from `core.transport` keeps that distinction visible in the import list — one moves
material, the other moves a number to a screen.

## XIV.4 The node — inventory, pressure and level

Vapour space:

$$
\frac{dP}{dt} \;=\; \frac{RT}{V_v}\,\bigl(\dot n_{\text{gen}} - \dot n_{\text{out}}\bigr)
\;+\; \frac{P}{T}\frac{dT}{dt}
\;-\; \frac{P}{V_v}\frac{dV_v}{dt},
\qquad
V_v = V_{\text{vessel}} - \frac{M_l}{\rho_l}
$$

Liquid space:

$$
M_{k+1} \;=\; \max\!\left(M_k + \frac{\dot m_{\text{in}} - \dot m_{\text{out}}}{3600}\,\Delta t,\; 1\ \mathrm{kg}\right)
$$

**Term by term.** The molar term needs **moles**, not mass. The failure it replaced was one
lumped $K = 0.02$ bar/(kg·s) shared by nine vessels — a 0.46 bar a vacuum separator and a
16.8 bar a hydrolyser on the same coefficient, with ammonia (MW 17) and carbon dioxide
(MW 44) treated as the same gas. The thermal term is why heating a blocked-in vapour space
raises its pressure with no molar change at all. The swell term is the coupling a lumped
capacitance throws away: a filling vessel gets a **stiffer** pressure response, which is
what puts a level excursion on the pressure transmitter.

The 1 kg floor is numerical, not a process claim. A vessel's species balance divides by its
inventory; at exactly zero, one tick of noise becomes a NaN that propagates through the
train. Against a 3000 kg design holdup it is 0.03 %. Emptying is represented by the level
reaching zero and the trip acting on it, never by the inventory state reaching zero.

Level indication is **anchored**, not volumetric:

$$
L\,[\%] \;=\; \mathrm{clamp}\!\left(\frac{M}{M_{\text{NLL}}}\,L_{\text{NLL}},\; 0,\; 100\right)
$$

`References/Datasheets` gives shell volumes and tapping elevations but no head-versus-volume
curve for a dished-end vessel with internals, so the anchored form is what the source data
supports and the volumetric one would be invented geometry.

## XIV.5 The published stream record

Both composition bases are derived from **one** per-component kmol/h vector:

$$
\dot m_i = \dot n_i M_i, \qquad
x_i = \frac{\dot n_i}{\sum_j \dot n_j}, \qquad
w_i = \frac{\dot m_i}{\sum_j \dot m_j}
$$

so a stream cannot be 38.6 % nitrogen by mole on one line of the display and by mass on the
next. Enthalpy is published on the **H0** tier with its basis declared per record; an
explicit override is published as **H2**, plant-reconciled.

**Two molar-mass tables, and the reason.** `core/stream.py` carries `MW_COMP`, which is
**atom-consistent** for the reactor couples:

$$
\mathrm{CO_2} + 2\,\mathrm{NH_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{Urea} + \mathrm{H_2O},
\qquad
2\,\mathrm{Urea} \rightarrow \mathrm{Biuret} + \mathrm{NH_3},
\qquad
\sum_i \nu_i M_i = 0 \ \text{exactly}
$$

so a reacting node closes its mass balance to machine zero. It differs in the last digits of
urea and biuret from `thermo.enthalpy.MOLAR_MASS`, which is fitted to calorimetric data.
`make_stream` re-specifies the mass-specific enthalpy against its **own** mass total, so the
two conventions never mix inside one record.

**A mole-per-cent row read as mass per cent is a real error, not a rounding one.** Every
vapour row in the PFD is tabulated on a mole basis. Read as mass, stream 706 publishes an
average molar weight of 22.38 against the PFD's own 24.13 — which is why the two
constructors are separate functions rather than one function with a flag.

## XIV.6 Two limiters, and two atmospheres

V1 defines `clamp` twice, and the two differ **only on a NaN** — which is exactly the input
a collapsing plant produces:

| source | form | a NaN gives |
|---|---|---|
| `main.py` | `max(lo, min(hi, x))` | `hi` |
| `consequence.py` | `lo if x < lo else (hi if x > hi else x)` | `NaN` |

Both are ported, each named for its behaviour. The consequence layer converts a deviation
into a **rate**, and there a NaN pinned to the upper bound would read as "fully open" on a
restriction fraction and hide the defect that produced it.

Likewise two atmospheric pressures: **1.013 bar** inside process relations — it sets the
SV-32201 relief at 161.013 bar a and the SV-32253 at 31.013 bar a — and **1.01325 bar** for
gauge indications, since every V1 screen reads `bara − 1.01325`. Both are load bearing, in
opposite directions, so both are kept under separate names, and a value converted with the
display constant must never re-enter a process relation. Handoff B-6.

## XIV.7 The flowsheet graph

The one module here with no V1 counterpart, and it contains no physics.

A urea synthesis loop is cyclic by construction — 322F001 → 322E002 → 322R001 → 322E003 →
322F001 — and a cyclic graph has no evaluation order. Every simulator of a recycle plant
must cut the loop somewhere and take the torn value from the previous tick. That cut is a
**modelling decision**: it sets which quantity is slightly late during a fast transient.

So `Flowsheet.evaluation_order()` removes the declared tears, runs Kahn's algorithm with
registration-order tie-breaking — deterministic, because a tick's floating-point result
depends on the order its terms are summed in — and **raises** on any remaining cycle, naming
the units still in it. A cycle with a declared tear is fine; a cycle without one is refused
rather than ordered arbitrarily, because an arbitrary order works on a developer's machine
and is wrong on the plant.

The 39 tears V1 actually uses are listed in `docs/step_sim_dataflow.md` §2, with twelve more
identified in `docs/coupling_resolution.md` that V1 hides inside `s.tlag.get()` calls.

---

# Part XV — The control layer

Seven modules in `ureasim/control`, plus the node balance that went to `core`. Everything
here is a DCS function or a piece of hardware it drives. Nothing here knows which equipment
it is attached to: a level controller does not know it is on 323F004. The unit supplies the
tag, the tuning and the design point; this layer supplies the law.

## XV.1 Two regulatory controllers, deliberately

V1 carries two velocity I-PD implementations **and uses both**. They are not duplicates, and
merging them would change the behaviour of one set of loops or the other.

| | `control/process_loop.ProcessLoop` | `control/controller.Controller` |
|---|---|---|
| V1 source | `main.py` `_ctrl_ipd` | `backend/controllers.py` |
| used on | every tag except two | SIC-321950, SIC-321951 |
| PV units | engineering (°C, bar a, % level, t/h) | per cent of span |
| bad-PV test | non-finite only | non-finite **or** outside $[-5, 105]\,\%$ |
| on a bad PV | freeze output, stay in mode | freeze output **and drop to MAN** |
| output slew limit | none | $\text{rate}\cdot\Delta t$ per tick |
| modes | MAN / AUTO / CAS | MAN / AUTO / CAS / OOS |
| $T_d < 0$ | sentinel: derivative disabled | used as given |
| PV history in MAN | kept current | frozen |

The two rows that matter most are the bad-PV test and the mode demotion. A reactor reading
183 °C is a perfectly good measurement; the per-cent-span controller would declare it failed,
drop the loop to MAN and freeze the valve on a plant that is running normally. That is why
the engineering-unit form exists, and it is why the merge is not available.

Both share the same increment (Part VIII.1). The engineering-unit form applies it as

$$
\Delta u = a\,K_c\big[-(PV_k - PV_{k-1}) + I(SP, PV) + D(PV)\big],
\qquad
u \leftarrow \operatorname{clamp}(u + \Delta u,\ u_{lo},\ u_{hi})
$$

with $a = \pm 1$ the direction of action, and

$$
I = \begin{cases} 0 & |SP - PV| < D_z \\ \dfrac{\Delta t}{T_i}(SP - PV) & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
\qquad
D = \begin{cases}
-T_d\,\dfrac{PV_k - 2PV_{k-1} + PV_{k-2}}{\Delta t} & T_f \le 0 \\[2ex]
G_k - G_{k-1},\ \ G_k = \dfrac{T_f}{T_f+\Delta t}G_{k-1} - \dfrac{T_d}{T_f+\Delta t}(PV_k - PV_{k-1}) & T_f > 0
\end{cases}
$$

The filtered branch collapses to the unfiltered one as $T_f \to 0$, to first order in
$T_f/\Delta t$ — asserted as a convergence, not checked at one arbitrary value — so the
default $T_f = 0$ is genuinely inert rather than merely small.

**The $T_d = -1$ sentinel.** The DCS writes $T_d = -1$ to mean *derivative disabled*;
FIC-324401 carries it. Taken as a number it flips the sign of the derivative term and injects
a wrong-way kick into the valve on every transient. V1 clamps $T_d < 0$ to zero, so the
sentinel is honoured exactly. The port does the same, and a test pins it against a literal
$-1$, which produces a visibly different trajectory.

**Seeding.** Every loop is seeded $pv = sp = pv_1 = pv_2$ at its design point, so the first
tick computes $\Delta u = 0$ and the boot fixed point is preserved to the bit. That is Rule 1
of Part 0, applied to a controller.

## XV.2 The valve laws — IEC 60534-2-1

Installed characteristic, at fractional stroke $h \in [0,1]$:

$$
\frac{C_v(h)}{C_{v,\max}} =
\begin{cases}
R^{\,h-1},\ R = 50 & \text{equal percentage} \\
h & \text{linear} \\
\sqrt{h} & \text{quick opening}
\end{cases}
$$

with a hard zero at $h = 0$, because $R^{-1}$ is $2\,\%$ and a shut valve does not leak two
per cent. The limiter is V1's own `min(max(h, 0), 1)` rather than the shared `clamp`: the two
disagree on a NaN stroke — this form propagates it, `clamp` returns $1.0$, a wide-open valve —
and a NaN stroke is exactly what a diverging controller produces.

Liquid service, with the flashing / cavitating limit:

$$
w = N_6\,F_p\,C_v(h)\sqrt{\Delta P_{\text{eff}}\,\rho_1},
\qquad
\Delta P_{\text{eff}} = \min\big(P_1 - P_2,\ F_L^2 (P_1 - F_F P_v)\big),
\qquad N_6 = 27.3
$$

Compressible service, with the expansion factor and the hard choke:

$$
F_\gamma = \frac{\gamma}{1.40},\qquad
x = \min\!\Big(\frac{\Delta P}{P_1},\ F_\gamma x_T\Big),\qquad
Y = \max\!\Big(1 - \frac{x}{3F_\gamma x_T},\ \frac{2}{3}\Big)
$$

$$
w = N_8\,F_p\,C_v(h)\,P_1\,Y\sqrt{\frac{x M}{T_1 Z}},\qquad N_8 = 94.8
$$

The $\min$ **is** the choke. Once $\Delta P/P_1$ reaches $F_\gamma x_T$, $x$ stops rising, $Y$
sits at $2/3$, and the flow depends on $P_2$ not at all. HV-322604 runs at
$\Delta P/P_1 = 0.97$ against an $F_\gamma x_T$ of about $0.70$ — deeply choked — and the
incompressible law it replaces had flow still climbing as the downstream pressure fell.

### XV.2.1 The anchored ratio, and why a back-solved $C_v$ is not enough

`References/Datasheets` holds no control-valve datasheet, so $C_{v,\max}$ is **back-solved**
from the licensor's design duty: the PFD flow, the design stroke and the design pressures on
both sides. But inverting $w = N_6 F_p C_v \phi \sqrt{\Delta P \rho}$ for $C_v$ and
multiplying straight back through does not return the original float — V1 measured
$101490.00000000001$ against $101490.0$ — and the boot pin asserts the design point to the
last bit. A 1-ulp drift at every valve on every tick is how a six-hour run walks off its
anchor.

So the engine calls the **ratio of the law to itself at the design condition**:

$$
w = w_{\text{des}}\cdot\frac{\Phi(\text{live})}{\Phi(\text{design})},
\qquad
\Phi_{\text{liq}} = C_v(h)\sqrt{\Delta P_{\text{eff}}\,\rho},
\qquad
\Phi_{\text{gas}} = C_v(h)\,P_1\,Y\sqrt{\frac{xM}{T_1Z}}
$$

$N_6$, $N_8$, $F_p$ and $C_{v,\max}$ are identical above and below, so they cancel
**algebraically** — which also means the absent valve datasheets stop mattering: the answer
never depended on $C_{v,\max}$ at all. What survives is every term a frozen
$\text{design}\times(\text{stroke}/\text{stroke}_{\text{des}})$ form is missing: the installed
characteristic, the live density, the live $\Delta P$ from node pressures on both sides, and
the choke. At design, numerator and denominator are the same expression on the same operands,
the bracket is exactly $1.0$, and $w = w_{\text{des}}$ bit-exact.

### XV.2.2 Two $F_F$ conventions, both preserved

The **absolute** liquid law holds $F_F$ at its intercept $0.96$, which is $F_F$ only in the
$P_v \ll P_c$ limit. The **anchored** form the engine calls evaluates the correlation in full:

$$
F_F = 0.96 - 0.28\sqrt{\frac{P_v}{P_c}},\qquad P_c = 220.64\ \text{bar (IAPWS, water)}
$$

A 190 °C liquor at 15 bar a has $F_F = 0.887$, so the two forms choke at different
differentials. This is V1's own inconsistency, it is load bearing at the sites that call each
form, and both are ported unchanged. A test fails if they are ever harmonised.

### XV.2.3 Gravity discharge and the non-return valve

$$
\Delta P = (P_{\text{vessel}} - P_{\text{dest}}) + \frac{\rho\,g\,h}{10^{5}}\ \ [\text{bar}]
$$

fed to the liquid valve law. As the level goes to zero the head term goes to zero, so the flow
goes to zero on its own — which is why V1's `if level <= 0` guards could be deleted rather
than ported.

$$
w = w_{\text{des}}\sqrt{\frac{P_{up} - P_{down} - P_{\text{crack}}}{\Delta P_{\text{des}} - P_{\text{crack}}}}
\quad\text{forward},\qquad w = 0\ \text{otherwise}
$$

Three properties define a check valve and all three matter: it is a fixed **resistance**
forward, so it can pass more than design when the line pushes harder (a
$\min(1,\sqrt{\Delta P/\Delta P_{\text{des}}})$ delivery fraction cannot); it is **shut**
across the whole crack band, not merely passing very little; and reverse flow is **exactly
zero** because the disc is seated, not because a square root went imaginary.

The anchor is bit-exact when $P_{up} - P_{down} - P_{\text{crack}}$ evaluates to the same
float as $\Delta P_{\text{des}} - P_{\text{crack}}$. Decimal plant pressures do not oblige:
$5.60 - 4.20$ is $1.4000000000000004$. A unit module must therefore derive
$\Delta P_{\text{des}}$ as the subtraction of its two design pressures, never as a rounded
decimal. Handoff A-13.

## XV.3 The flow loop, and the volumetric migration

A flow control valve and its transmitter form the fastest loop on the plant. The model is the
simplest thing that is still a proper loop: a pure gain from stroke to flow, and a measurement
that is that flow lagged by the transmitter's time constant.

$$
w_{\text{pre}} = w_{\text{des}}\frac{u_{k-1}}{u_{\text{des}}},
\qquad
PV = \text{lag}_\tau(w_{\text{pre}}),
\qquad
w = w_{\text{des}}\frac{u_k}{u_{\text{des}}}
$$

Lagging the **measurement** and not the flow is what makes the loop first order with
$|z| < 1$ — stable for any tuning a trainee can dial in — while leaving the delivered flow
instantaneous, which is what the downstream mass balance must receive. At design
$u = u_{\text{des}} \Rightarrow w_{\text{pre}} = w_{\text{des}} \Rightarrow PV = SP \Rightarrow
\Delta u = 0$: bit-exact.

**Consequence for the flowsheet.** A FIC in AUTO holds its leg at set point by integral
action, so it *rejects* any element placed in series with it. An upstream level valve must
**cascade into** the FIC, never be modelled by derating $w_{\text{des}}$ — otherwise it has no
steady-state authority and winds up.

FIC-323401, FIC-328405 and FIC-323418 run **volumetrically**: the field element meters volume,
so the controller compares m³/h against m³/h. The lagged mass PV and any cascade set point are
divided by $\rho$ before the controller sees them. The retune keeps the closed loop invariant
— the open-loop gain scales as $g_{\text{vol}} = g_{\text{mass}}/\rho$, so
$K_{c,\text{vol}} = K_{c,\text{mass}}\,\rho$ leaves $K_c g$ unchanged, and
$K_c(\Delta t/T_i)\varepsilon$ is unchanged because the error scales the other way, so $T_i$
stays. The **return is always mass**, so no downstream balance is touched by the choice of
loop units.

## XV.4 Ratio control, and external-reset feedback

$$
r_{PV} = \frac{w_{\text{dosed}}}{w_{\text{base}}},
\qquad
SP_{\text{slave}} = \max\big(r_{\text{cmd}}\cdot w_{\text{base}},\ 0\big)
$$

and, open loop, where the ratio is a set point rather than a controlled variable:

$$
w_{\text{demand}} = r_{SP}\cdot f\cdot w_{\text{base}},
\qquad f = \frac{M_{NH_3}}{M_{CO_2}}\ \text{for the N/C feed ratio}
$$

— a molar ratio commanding a mass flow has to cross that bridge.

Two behaviours make it a control block rather than a multiplication, and both exist to stop
the master integrating against something it cannot influence:

* **external-reset feedback.** While the slave is not in cascade, nothing the master computes
  reaches a valve. An integrating master would ramp to its limit and dump that output onto the
  plant the moment cascade was restored. Instead an AUTO master **tracks the achieved ratio**,
  so its output is always the ratio the plant is actually making and the transfer is bumpless.
  A master deliberately left in MAN keeps the operator's number; only its PV history advances.
* **freeze on a permissive.** When a hard interlock has zeroed the dosing pump, the ratio is
  zero because the equipment is stopped. The master is frozen rather than stepped, and the
  measurement decays toward zero on its own transmitter so no faceplate claims a flow that is
  not being delivered.

## XV.5 Latching interlocks

The module decides whether a trip is **latched**. It does not stop a pump, shut a valve or
force a controller to manual: a trip's action list is plant knowledge and belongs to the unit
that owns the equipment, and the same action is commanded by several trips.

Four rules, one per trip shape:

| shape | rule | trips |
|---|---|---|
| plain | latch on a live initiator; reset only once it has cleared | 21.2, 21.8, 21.10 |
| armed | latch only while an arming condition also holds | 21.4 |
| reset-banded | latch at $P \ge P_{\text{trip}}$; while latched the live condition is $P \ge P_{\text{reset}}$ | 22.2 |
| self-clearing | latch above a high limit, clear below a lower one, no operator reset | 22.1 |

with $P_{\text{trip}} = 155.0$ bar a and $P_{\text{reset}} = 148.0$ bar a for 22.2, and
$57.0$ °C set / $55.0$ °C clear for 22.1.

**Arming** is what stops a trip latching itself out of a black start: 21.4's initiator — no
CO₂ — is trivially true on a plant that has not started, so it latches only while synthesis is
actually running. **The reset band** is what stops a plant being reset onto the edge of the
condition it just tripped on. **Self-clearing** applies to 22.1 alone, because it is a
protective action rather than a shutdown: it floods the absorber with steam while it is hot
and hands the valve back when it cools, and there is no reset control for it on the overlay.

A reset returns whether it actually cleared, because V1 resolves a pump's mechanical fault on
a **successful** reset only — so that "reset" means *cause resolved* rather than *annunciator
silenced*, and a refused reset resolves nothing.

At design every initiator is false: $T_{c001} \approx 43$ °C, $P_{\text{syn}} = 140.7$ bar a.
The trip block therefore contributes nothing at the boot pin.

## XV.6 The centrifugal compressor

$$
\frac{n-1}{n} = \frac{k-1}{k\,\eta_p},
\qquad
H = N_s\,\frac{Z_1 R T_1}{M}\cdot\frac{n}{n-1}\left[\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{nN_s}} - 1\right],
\qquad
T_2 = T_1\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{nN_s}}
$$

Intercooling makes the head sum **linear** in the stage count instead of exponential in the
overall ratio, and it also fixes the machine's sensitivity to back pressure: an uncooled
single section is far stiffer than the real train, and one running from 1.6 to 144 bar would
discharge above 870 °C — arithmetic right, machine wrong.

In fan-law reduced coordinates one curve describes every speed:

$$
q = \frac{Q_{in}/Q_{in,\text{des}}}{N/N_{\text{des}}},
\qquad
\psi = \frac{H/H_{\text{des}}}{(N/N_{\text{des}})^2},
\qquad
\psi(q) = 1 + a_1(q-1) + a_2(q-1)^2
$$

with $a_1, a_2$ fitted to the two facts a datasheet states even when the full curve is absent
— the head rise to surge and the surge flow — so that the **peak of the parabola is the surge
line** and the design point is $(q,\psi) = (1,1)$ by construction. Inversion takes the larger
root: the smaller one lies on the positively-sloped branch, on which a centrifugal machine
cannot run steadily.

The delivered mass follows from the inlet density, $\rho_1 = P_1 M/(Z R T_1)$, because a
centrifugal machine is a **volumetric** device — which is why a suction pressure loss costs
throughput even when nothing about the machine has changed.

What this replaces is an algebraic assertion, $P_{\text{line}} = \min(P_{\text{syn}} +
\Delta P_{\text{des}},\ P_{\text{ceiling}})$ — a statement about the desired process outcome,
with no flow argument, so the machine could not be off its curve, could not surge, could not
stonewall and had no speed. None of those could be taught, because none of them could happen.

## XV.7 The pressure-node balance

$$
\text{residual}(P) = \text{supply}(P) - \sum_i \text{branch}_i(P) = 0
$$

Where a machine discharges into two or more destinations there is no split *fraction* to
assign. The branches meet at a node, the node has one pressure, and that pressure is whatever
makes delivery equal the sum of what the branches can pass. A normalised conductance ratio
$f = g_{HP}/(g_{HP}+g_{\text{vent}})$ forces the branch flows to sum to the supply by
construction, which cannot represent a vent wide open while the loop also draws hard, and
cannot let the node pressure fall below the destination pressure and shut a check valve on its
own.

The supply is monotonically decreasing in $P$ and each branch monotonically increasing, so the
residual is strictly decreasing and a bracketed bisection is unconditionally convergent: no
Jacobian, no initial-guess sensitivity, no chance of the wrong root. A Newton step would be
faster and would occasionally find a root that is not the physical one, which in an operator
trainer is the worse trade.

When the residual at the design seed is **exactly** zero the seed is returned unchanged —
bisection would otherwise land a few ulp away and unpin every constant downstream of it.

## XV.8 Every stated assumption in this layer, in one place

Rule 4 of Part 0 says no number without provenance. Four numbers in this layer are
**representative values, stated openly**, because the archive does not contain the datum and
inventing a vendor figure would be worse than declaring the gap:

| quantity | value | what it decides | why it is stated |
|---|---|---|---|
| $F_L$ | 0.90 | where a liquid valve starts to flash | IEC 60534-2-1 Table 1, globe valve, contoured plug, flow-to-open — the trim class every throttling service here is described as. No valve datasheets exist in either repository. |
| $x_T$ | 0.75 | where a gas valve chokes | same table, same caveat |
| $P_{\text{crack}}$ | per site | exactly where a check valve slams shut | no check-valve datasheet. Its influence is under 0.1 % of flow above half the design differential and it cancels exactly at design; what it fixes is the shut point, which nothing else fixes. |
| compressor map | $q_{\text{surge}} = 0.68$, head rise $0.12$, $q_{\text{stonewall}} = 1.20$ | surge and stonewall flags | no machine curve for 320K002. The design point is exact; the map supplies only the shape around it. |

All four are recorded in `handoff.md` §Open data gaps. $C_{v,\max}$ is **not** in this table,
because it is back-solved from the licensor's design duty and then cancels algebraically out
of every anchored call — the engine's answers do not depend on it.

# Part XVI — Unit 321: the NH3 pumping station

The first unit operation ported, and the pattern for the seven sections that follow. It is
also the smallest, which is why it went first: two machines, one drum, one ratio block, and
one stream leaving for the synthesis loop.

## XVI.1 What sets the plant rate

The operator sets a molar N/C. Everything else in this section follows from it:

$$
\dot m_{NH_3,sp} = \left(\frac{N}{C}\right)_{sp}\cdot\frac{M_{NH_3}}{M_{CO_2}}\cdot \dot m_{CO_2},
\qquad
Q_{sp} = \frac{\dot m_{NH_3,sp}}{\rho},
\qquad
N_{req} = \frac{Q_{sp}/n_{\text{active}}}{V_{\text{swept}}\,\eta_v\,60}
$$

$$
\text{opening}_{cas} = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\frac{N_{req}}{N_{\text{rated}}}\cdot 100,\ 0,\ 100\right)
$$

Three things in that chain are worth stating because they are not obvious:

**The demand is a SPEED, not a flow.** 321P002 A/B are triplex reciprocating
positive-displacement pumps. They sweep a fixed volume per revolution and deliver it against
whatever pressure the discharge is at, up to their relief. There is no head/flow curve to sit
on and nothing to throttle: closing the discharge valve on a running plunger pump raises the
pressure until something gives. Flow is changed by changing speed and only by changing speed.
This is why unit 321 has no counterpart to the compressor map in Part XV.6.

**The demand is per MACHINE.** Dividing by $n_{\text{active}}$ is what makes starting the
standby pump bumpless: two machines are each asked for half the speed, so the total delivery
does not change at the moment of the start. A cascade that commanded a total would double the
ammonia feed the instant the second machine came in.

**The controlled variable is an OPENING, not a speed.** Speed is set by a VOITH
torque-converter scoop, and what SIC-321950/951 can actually move is the converter's valve
opening in per cent. The speed is derived, $N = (\text{opening}/100)\,N_{\text{rated}}$, and
displayed separately on the pump tile. The controller's PV is the ACTUAL opening, so the
converter's own two-second lag sits inside the loop and the SIC has to drive through it.

At the design point the chain closes on itself exactly. $M_{CO_2}/M_{NH_3}$ and its
reciprocal multiply to $1.0$, so the design N/C against the design CO2 feed asks for the
opening the machine already has, the increment is zero, and the delivered motive flow is
`EJ_MOTIVE_NH3_DES` to the bit.

## XVI.2 The pump

$$
V_{\text{swept}} = \frac{\pi}{4}D^2 L\,n_{\text{plungers}},
\qquad
Q = N\,V_{\text{swept}}\,\eta_v\,60,
\qquad
P_{\text{shaft}} = \frac{Q\,\Delta P}{\eta_m}
$$

with $D = 140$ mm, $L = 205$ mm and three plungers, all from the datasheet.

**On $\eta_v$, and why the model departs from the datasheet capacity.** At the assumed
$\eta_v = 0.95$ the swept volume reproduces the datasheet's own 67.1 and 82 m3/h at 124 and
152 rpm, to 0.3 %. That agreement is the check that the GEOMETRY is right. The constant
actually used is the field-calibrated $\eta_v = 0.980$, fitted to a DCS startup trace
(3 June 2025, temperature-separated, $0.980 \pm 0.001$, $n = 5$, flat across 100-142 bar g),
which passes 69.0 and 84.6 m3/h instead.

That fit is **degenerate** and the model says so. FY-321401 was shown to be a fixed-constant
DCS compute tag — the 28 June warm-feed slope is $-0.07\,\%$ against $-2.1\,\%$ predicted for
a live density — so what the trace constrains is only the PRODUCT
$\eta_v\,\rho_{\text{cfg}} = 601.6$ kg/m3. Taking $0.980$ assumes
$\rho_{\text{cfg}} = \rho_{\text{sat}}(17.6\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}) = 613.9$. It is
conservation-neutral either way: $\eta_v$ cancels in the closed-loop ratio reconstruction —
the speed is back-computed and the mass rebuilt — so only the SIC-321950 rpm display shifts.

## XVI.3 The drum, and why its makeup is fed forward

321D003 is 0.97 m across and 1.4 m tall: about 1.03 m3, holding roughly 650 kg at the working
level against a pump draw of 42.8 t/h. **One minute of inventory.**

$$
\dot m_{BL} = \operatorname{clamp}\big(\dot m_{\text{draw}} + K_p (L_{sp} - L),\ 0,\ \dot m_{BL,\max}\big),
\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}M}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot m_{BL} - \dot m_{\text{draw}}
$$

The feed-forward term is not a refinement. A plain proportional controller on a one-minute
inventory either drains it into the 21.2 low-level trip or floods it on a feed disturbance,
because by the time the level has moved far enough to generate an error the inventory is
already gone. With the draw carried forward, import equals draw at steady state, the
proportional part is a correction rather than the whole signal, and the level holds at set
point with **zero offset**. At design the two cancel exactly and $\mathrm{d}M = 0$, which is
what keeps the boot pin bit-exact.

The energy balance is adiabatic — no heat input, negligible environmental loss against a
one-minute residence time:

$$
M c_p \frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot m_{BL}\,c_p\,(T_{BL} - T)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\dot m_{BL}(T_{BL} - T)}{M}
$$

$c_p$ cancels, which is why it does not appear in the code. Below one kilogram of inventory
the temperature is HELD rather than integrated: a drum with a kilogram in it has no bulk
temperature, and dividing by it gives an unbounded rate.

## XVI.4 The sub-cooling margin, which is a trip and not a diagnostic

$$
P_{\text{suct}} = P_{\text{top}} + \frac{\rho\,g\,L\,H}{10^{5}} - \Delta P_{\text{static}},
\qquad
PY = P_{\text{sat}}^{NH_3}(T),
\qquad
PDY = (P_{\text{feed}} + P_{\text{atm}}) - PY
$$

with the ammonia saturation pressure on the NIST Antoine form,

$$
\log_{10} P[\mathrm{bar}] = A - \frac{B}{T[\mathrm{K}] + C},
\qquad A = 4.86886,\ B = 1113.928,\ C = -10.409
$$

PDYI-321203/204 is an initiator of trip 21.2, the urea synthesis main trip, and it fires below
**0.1 bar**. A reciprocating pump handling liquid at its bubble point flashes it on the
suction stroke and knocks; the margin is what says the liquid is still liquid. Two quite
different upsets destroy it — the level falls, or the temperature rises — and one equation
catches both, which is why it is computed rather than inferred from either.

This is also why the drum runs at 12.3 bar g on 25 C ammonia, roughly 3 bar above its
saturation pressure, rather than at a storage condition.

**Two pressures, deliberately.** The physical suction head above is kept for the physics and
the trips. PT-321201/202 read something else — the NH3 FEED-STREAM pressure at the drum, that
is, the top operating pressure — because that is what the plant's own transmitters read. The
model carries both and does not substitute one for the other.

**Two gravities, deliberately.** The head term uses $g = 9.81$, V1's own constant here;
`consequence.py` uses standard gravity, 9.80665. The difference is $1.8\times10^{-5}$ bar at
the design level — four orders below the trip margin it feeds, and therefore exactly the kind
of difference that would never be found again if it were quietly harmonised. Both are carried
under separate names. Handoff B-7.

## XVI.5 The discharge, and the transit that follows it

$$
\Delta T_{\text{pump}} = \frac{\Delta P}{\rho c_p}\left[\beta T + \frac{1-\eta_h}{\eta_h}\right]
$$

Liquid ammonia arrives at the ejector hotter than it left the drum, and across roughly 152 bar
the rise is several kelvin — it sets the motive enthalpy the HP carbamate condenser receives.
Both terms in the bracket are carried: the reversible work of compressing an expansible liquid
($\beta T$), and the irreversible dissipation of whatever the hydraulic efficiency does not
convert. The first vanishes for a truly incompressible liquid and the second for a perfect
pump; neither is true.

The motive stream then crosses the battery limit:

$$
t_d = \frac{m_{\text{line}}}{\dot m}\cdot 3600,
\qquad
m_{\text{line}} = \dot m_{\text{des}}\,\frac{t_{d,\text{des}}}{3600} = 4098\ \mathrm{kg}
$$

$t_{d,\text{des}} = 345$ s is a MEASUREMENT — the PT-329201 FOPTD fit from the 3 June 2025 DCS
anchor set, $R^2 = 0.9888$, bracketed at or below 572 s. The line inventory is back-solved
from it rather than entered, so the two cannot disagree. What V1's predecessor had wrong was
not the number but that it did not MOVE: at half rate the transit doubles, and the delay is
re-timed through the timestamped FIFO of Part XIV.3, which conserves mass exactly because
every sample is emitted once.

The two fractions the synthesis loop is anchored on come out of the delayed stream:

$$
\varphi_m = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\frac{\dot m_{\text{motive}}}{\dot m_{\text{motive,des}}},\ 0,\ 1.5\right),
\qquad
\varphi_{\text{fwd}} = \varphi_m^2
$$

$\varphi_{\text{fwd}}$ is the affinity-law head fraction: the ejector's developed head, and
through it the HPCC-to-reactor circulation and the discharge header pressure, go as the square
of the motive flow. It is $1.0$ at design, so every hydraulic state downstream holds its
design value by construction.

*(This entry corrects `docs/coupling_resolution.md`, which had resolved $\varphi_{\text{fwd}}$
as an ejector spindle position from HIC-322602. It is not an actuator position; it is the
square of the motive-flow fraction. The row is now RESULT.)*

## XVI.6 The ratio PV, and its validity gate

$$
\frac{N}{C} = \frac{\dot m_{NH_3}}{\dot m_{CO_2}}\cdot\frac{M_{CO_2}}{M_{NH_3}}
= \frac{\dot m_{NH_3}}{\dot m_{CO_2}}\cdot 2.584
$$

published per machine and summed, so an operator can see which pump is contributing what.

Below **5 % of the design CO2 feed** the divisor collapses and a molar N/C is numerically
meaningless — an arbitrarily large number that says nothing about the plant. The published
value is then HELD at its last good reading and a bad flag is raised, which freezes the
cascade instead of propagating garbage into a set point. That is the behaviour on a black
start and on a loss of CO2 feed, and it is why an operator sees the ratio go BAD rather than
go wild. The per-machine split reported while the measurement is bad is half the held ratio
each, and is labelled by the same flag.

Note that the molar masses here — 17.031 and 44.009 — are the ratio block's own, and are NOT
the atom-consistent values `core.stream.MW_COMP` carries for the reactor couples (17.0304 and
44.0098). V1 carries both sets and uses each in its own place. Substituting either would move
a published number.

## XVI.7 Where the section ends

At the motive ammonia stream, after its transit, plus $\varphi_m$ and $\varphi_{\text{fwd}}$.
The 322F001 ejector is synthesis equipment and belongs to Part VII's 322 balances; unit 321
hands over the stream and stops, which is where the plant's own unit boundary is.

What comes IN from elsewhere is the live CO2 feed to the loop in t/h, computed by the 320K002
discharge node. The ratio block divides by it, which is why the section cannot be stepped
without it — and why the validity gate above exists at all.


---

# Part XVII — Unit 320: the CO2 feed compressor and its discharge line

Unit 321 sets the plant rate by *dividing* by the CO2 feed. This is the section that produces
that divisor. It is the rate-setting equipment on the site: 320K002 delivers the carbon, the
N/C ratio block follows it, and every ammonia flow downstream follows the ratio block.

Three pieces of equipment and one volume: the machine, the line it discharges into, the
XV-322902 tie-in with its non-return valve, and PV-322203, the line vent to the LP safe
header under PIC-322203.

## XVII.1 The machine, and why every one of its anchors is derived

320K002 is a four-section intercooled centrifugal machine taking CO2 from the ammonia plant's
battery limit at 1.6 bar a and 40 °C and putting it into the loop at 144.2 bar a — about 90:1
overall. The map itself is Part XV's `CentrifugalMap` / `CentrifugalCompressor`; what unit 320
adds is the anchoring, and the anchoring is written as a *chain of derivations* so the machine
and the duty cannot be made to disagree by editing one of them:

$$
n = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma - (\gamma-1)\,\eta_p},
\qquad
\rho_{in,des} = \frac{P_{suct}\,M}{Z R T_{suct}},
\qquad
Q_{in,des} = \frac{\dot m_{des}}{\rho_{in,des}},
$$

$$
H_{p,des} \;=\; n_{st}\cdot\frac{n}{n-1}\,\frac{RT_{suct}}{M}
\left[\left(\frac{P_{disch}}{P_{suct}}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{n\,n_{st}}}-1\right]
$$

with $n_{st}=4$ equal-ratio sections. Not one of $Q_{in,des}$, $H_{p,des}$ or
$\rho_{in,des}$ is entered as a number: they are computed from the licensor's design duty at
import time. `q_in_des` comes out at **20 568.62 m³/h** and `head_des` at **320.37 kJ/kg**,
against V1's stated 320.4.

**Why four sections and not one.** 90:1 on a single uncooled section discharges above 870 °C,
which is arithmetic rather than a machine. Four equal-ratio sections put the last-stage
discharge near 160 °C and the aftercooler takes it to the 120 °C the PFD carries as the feed
temperature.

The consequence of the derivation chain is the property Rule 1 exists for: at speed 1.0 into
144.2 bar a the reduced flow $q$ is exactly 1, so $\psi(q)$ is exactly 1, so the machine
returns exactly `CO2_DES_KGH`. The design point is bit-exact, and the fitted map shape — surge
at $q=0.68$, 12 % head rise to surge, stonewall at $q=1.20$ — supplies only the curvature
*around* it. Those three are a **stated assumption**: no vendor curve for 320K002 exists in
`References/Datasheets`, which holds vessel, exchanger and pump datasheets only. They are
declared in `handoff.md` §Open data gaps, in the same class as `FL_GLOBE` and `XT_GLOBE`.

## XVII.2 The governor, and why an open-loop map diverges on this flowsheet

A compressor map on its own is open loop: the machine sits wherever its curve and the back
pressure put it. On this flowsheet that is not merely imprecise, it is **divergent**, and V1
measured the divergence at 140.7 → 134.7 bar a over 16 000 s, monotonic and accelerating.

The mechanism is a positive feedback loop through the synthesis inventory, and every link of
it is real process behaviour:

1. the loop pressure falls a little, so the discharge node falls;
2. a lower discharge pressure is *less* head, so the machine rides **up** its curve and
   delivers **more** CO2;
3. the extra CO2 condenses into carbamate, so it leaves the vapour space;
4. less vapour is less pressure — return to step 1.

Nothing in the open-loop model opposes it. On the real plant the machine is flow controlled: a
governor trims speed — inlet guide vanes on some trains — to hold the demanded rate against
whatever discharge pressure the loop presents. That is what breaks the loop on the plant, so
it is what breaks it here:

$$
N \;\leftarrow\; \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(N + \frac{\Delta t}{\tau_{gov}}\cdot
\frac{\dot m_{dem} - \dot m_{del,k-1}}{\dot m_{des}},\; 0,\; N_{max}\right),
\qquad \tau_{gov} = 8\ \text{s},\ N_{max} = 1.15
$$

Two details are deliberate. The error is **normalised on the design flow**, so $\tau_{gov}$ is
in seconds and means the same thing at every load. And the delivery term is the **previous**
tick's, which is a declared recycle tear, not an oversight: reading this tick's delivery would
close an algebraic loop with the node solve below it, because the delivery depends on the node
pressure and the node pressure depends on the delivery. At design the demand and the delivery
are the same number, the increment is a literal 0.0, and the speed holds exactly 1.0.

There is a ceiling and no floor below zero. A governor cannot drive a machine backwards.

## XVII.3 The line is a vessel, and it is integrated rather than solved

The discharge line holds **5234.2 kg** of CO2 in **21.566 m³** and behaves exactly like a small
vessel. Both numbers come from one measurement and are *constrained* by each other rather than
fitted independently: the DCS-measured 345 s feed dead time back-solves the inventory at the
design flow, and the PFD line density at 144.2 bar a and 120 °C turns that inventory into a
volume. A line holding $M$ kg has **both** a transport lag $M/\dot m$ and a capacitance
$RT/(V M_{bar})$ with $V = M/\rho$. Deriving both from one inventory is physics, not a second
free parameter — and if the real run length ever turns up, it replaces the back-solve and both
follow it.

The node uses the same equation every vessel in the plant uses, so a line node and a vessel
node cannot drift apart in convention:

$$
\frac{dP}{dt} \;=\; \frac{R\,T_{line}}{V_{line}}\left(\dot n_{machine} - \dot n_{check} -
\dot n_{vent}\right)
$$

$T_{line}$ is the aftercooled feed temperature and is a boundary, so its $dT/dt$ term is a
literal 0.0; the line holds no liquid, so the swell term is a literal 0.0 as well.

**Why integrated and not solved algebraically.** V1 first wrote the algebraic form —
`machines.solve_node_pressure` on this node — and measured it diverging: 140.70 → 135.16 bar a
over 16 000 s. The diagnosis is that a *massless* node must satisfy its mass balance
instantaneously, which makes the branch far stiffer than the plant and hands the synthesis
loop's own pressure integrator a slow one-way term. A real discharge line is not massless.

**What this replaced.** The predecessor made two assertions about the process *outcome* and
called them a model. `P_line = min(P_syn + dP_des, P_ceiling)` — "the compressor always
delivers exactly the design differential until it cannot" — contains no flow argument, so it
has no operating point. And `f_to_HP = g_HP/(g_HP + g_vent)` with $g=\sqrt{\Delta P}$ forces
the two branch flows to sum to the raw feed *by construction*, so it cannot represent a vent
wide open while the loop also draws hard, and it cannot let the node fall below the loop and
shut the tie-in on its own.

The steady state the integrated node settles on is the same statement the algebraic float used
to assert — at the design differential the check valve passes the machine's delivery, so
$P_{line}$ tracks $p_{syn} + 3.5$ — but it is now an **outcome** of a mass balance rather than
an axiom. Three behaviours the axiom could not produce come with it: the line lags by about
13 s on the check valve's own gain; the tie-in **shuts** on reversal instead of merely passing
zero; and the deliverable ceiling is the machine running out of head rather than a `min()`
against a process design pressure. That last one matters for two protection layers the old
ceiling made dead — the 151.2 bar a line relief, and the loss-of-condensation chain, which
used to self-choke its own CO2 feed and so could never reach the high-high trip.

## XVII.4 The two branches, and the differential that must be a subtraction

The tie-in is a **check valve**, on Part XV's anchored law:

$$
\dot m_{check} = f_{XV}\cdot \dot m_{des}\sqrt{\frac{\Delta P - \Delta P_{crack}}
{\Delta P_{des} - \Delta P_{crack}}},
\qquad \Delta P = P_{line} - p_{syn}
$$

forward with **no ceiling** — a line pushing harder than design really does pass more — and a
hard zero both below the crack pressure and in reverse, because the disc is on its seat. When
the synthesis loop over-pressures past the CO2 line the feed stops rather than reversing into
the compressor. $f_{XV}$ is XV-322902, 1.0 open and 0.0 shut; it **multiplies** rather than
gates, so an isolated line still integrates its own pressure correctly with no draw.

$\Delta P_{des}$ is written as

$$
\Delta P_{des} = P_{CO_2,des} - P_{syn,des} = 144.2 - 140.7
$$

**as a subtraction, never as a literal 3.5.** This is handoff A-13. The anchored form returns
$\dot m_{des}$ to the last bit only when the live differential evaluates to the *same
IEEE-754 double* as the design one, and decimal plant pressures do not oblige: at a site
anchored on `5.60 - 4.20` the subtraction is `1.4000000000000004`, the literal is `1.40`, and
the valve returns `37999.99999999999` against a design duty of `38000.0`.

**This particular site is the benign case, and that is stated rather than glossed over.**
`144.2 - 140.7` happens to evaluate to exactly `3.5`, so the literal would have been bit-exact
here too. The rule is written down now, while the only site that exists is one that cannot
fail it, precisely because the next one carries no such luck — and because V1 already writes
this differential as a subtraction, so following it costs nothing.

The crack pressure is 2 % of that same differential — a
**stated assumption**, since no check-valve datasheet exists — expressed as a fraction so it
scales with the site rather than being a bare number.

The vent is a real compressible valve on the anchored IEC 60534 law of Part XV, linear trim
because this is vent duty rather than throttling, and it chokes as it should: 144 bar a down to
a 5 bar a header is a pressure ratio of 0.035, deeply choked at any meaningful opening. Its
anchor is the valve **wide open at the design line pressure passing the design CO2 rate** —
that is, sized to take the whole machine — which is what makes it a protection layer rather
than a trim.

The effective opening is

$$
\text{opening} = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\max\left(\text{HIC-322203},\ \text{PIC-322203}_{op}\right),\ 0,\ 100\right)
$$

so the operator's hand station can force the vent **open** but cannot force it shut.

## XVII.5 PIC-322203, and the V1 defect it is not ported with

The vent controller is the same velocity I-PD as every other loop, direct acting so that a
rising line pressure opens the vent:

$$
\Delta u = K_c\left[(PV - PV_{k-1}) + \frac{\Delta t}{T_i}(PV - SP)\right],
\qquad K_c = 1.0,\ T_i = 2\ \text{s}
$$

That is `control.process_loop.ProcessLoop` with $\sigma = -1$ and no derivative, term for term,
and the rewrite installs it as exactly that (`co2_line.vent_pressure_loop`). Negating the gain
and both terms is exact in IEEE arithmetic, so on every finite measurement the installed loop is
V1's inline block to the bit; the equivalence test drives the two side by side over 500 ticks
that swing across the set point and drive the stroke onto both rails. The set point is
derived, not entered:

$$
SP = P_{PSV} + 2\,\Delta P_{des} = 161.013 + 2(144.2-140.7) \approx 168.0\ \text{bar a}
$$

well above the operating line pressure, so the vent is shut at design and the loop acts only
on a genuine line over-pressure.

The operator's set point is clamped to $[120, 175]$ bar a, V1's own span from the `pic_set`
branch of `handle_cmd`, which applies it to an entered set point and to the bumpless
set-point-to-PV transfer on entering AUTO alike.

**The one decided divergence: a bad measurement.** V1's inline block skips the increment on a
non-finite PV but advances $PV_{k-1}$ regardless, so the NaN is carried into the next tick's
proportional term. V1's limiter `max(lo, min(hi, x))` returns $hi$ for a NaN, so a single
non-finite line pressure latches the vent **wide open** one tick after the measurement
recovers, and the loop then walks it back down at its own integral rate — a spike to fully
open and a slow recovery, easy to miss on a trend and a real CO2 loss.

The port first reproduced this and logged it for the process engineer (formerly handoff B-8),
because Rule 5 forbids improving a ported relation on the rewrite's own authority. **Decided
2026-09-26: PIC-322203 is installed as a `ProcessLoop`.** On a bad sample it freezes the output
AND the history, so the recovered measurement is compared with the last GOOD one:

$$
PV_k \notin \mathbb{R} \;\Rightarrow\; u_k = u_{k-1},\quad
(PV_{k-1}, PV_{k-2}) \text{ unchanged}
$$

A bad sample therefore costs exactly one tick of control action. After it the loop is, to the
bit, the loop that never saw the sample, and the test proves that by running the two side by
side. The loop stays in the mode the operator left it in: `ProcessLoop` has no bad-PV demotion
to MAN (that belongs to the per-cent-of-span `Controller`), so none is claimed here.

What this costs is V1 equivalence on that one path, and nothing else: at design and on every
finite trajectory the stroke is V1's to the bit. The equivalence test asserts both sides of the
divergence — V1's stroke going to 100.0 on the recovered sample and the rewrite's staying at 0.0
— so the record is what the difference is, not only that the rewrite is well behaved.

The PV is written at the **end** of a tick from that tick's settled line pressure and read at
the **top** of the next one. The loop therefore acts on a one-tick-old measurement by
construction. That is a declared tear, not a scheduling accident.

## XVII.6 Tick order, and why the branches are evaluated twice

The order within a tick is the plant's own and is not interchangeable:

1. **PIC-322203** steps on the stored measurement, and the effective vent opening is formed;
2. the **governor** trims speed on the previous tick's delivery;
3. the **machine** delivers into the *previous* node pressure, and that delivery becomes the
   governor's tear for next tick;
4. the **node balance** is formed from the two branch flows evaluated **at the previous
   pressure**, and integrated;
5. the two branch flows are evaluated **again, at the settled pressure**, and *those* are what
   is published;
6. the transit lag is applied and the new measurement is published to the controller.

Steps 4 and 5 are the same two functions called twice with different arguments, deliberately.
Using the settled pressure in the balance would make the integration implicit in its own
result; using the previous pressure in the report would publish a flow the line did not pass.

The transit at the end is the plug-flow law of Part V on the line's own inventory:

$$
t_d = \frac{M_{line}}{\dot m},\qquad \text{capped at } t_{d,max}
$$

so the CO2 the loop receives *now* left the battery-limit meter up to 345 s ago — while
FT-322403 and FY-322403 read the **live** meter, which is why the indications are computed
before the lag is applied and not after.

## XVII.7 Design closure

Closure at the design point is exact and by construction, not to a tolerance. At
$P_{line} = 144.2$ and $p_{syn} = 140.7$:

* the check valve sees exactly $\Delta P_{des}$, so its ratio is a literal 1.0 and it passes
  exactly `CO2_DES_KGH`;
* the vent at zero opening passes exactly 0;
* the map at speed 1.0 into 144.2 bar a returns exactly `CO2_DES_KGH`;
* therefore the node imbalance is a literal 0.0, and so is $dP/dt$.

One tick from the design seed leaves the pressure at 144.2 bar a unchanged, the feed at
**54.618 t/h**, the vent at 0.0, the load at **100.0 %** and the speed at exactly 1.0.

## XVII.8 Where the section ends

At the CO2 fed through XV-322902 into 322E001, in t/h, both live and transit-delayed, plus the
line pressure, the vent flow, the machine's surge and stonewall flags and the plant load.

Unit 321's ratio block divides by the **live** feed — which is the coupling that makes the two
sections inseparable at run time and is why the ratio block carries a validity gate below 5 %
of design feed. The **delayed** stream is what the synthesis loop itself receives. Publishing
both, with the transit time alongside them, is what lets an operator see a CO2 upset in the
ratio indication several minutes before the reactor feels it.


---

# Part XVIII — Unit 322E001: the HP CO2 stripper

The unit that makes a CO2-stripping plant a CO2-stripping plant. The reactor converts a little
over half its carbon per pass, and everything it did not convert has to come back. 322E001 is
what sends it back **at loop pressure**, instead of letting it down to the LP section and
paying a compressor to bring it up again.

Physically: 2600 tubes, 6 m effective, OD 31 x 3 mm, 1519 m2, 39.4 MW. Reactor liquor enters
the tube top and runs down the wall as a falling film; CO2 sweep gas enters the tube bottom and
rises through it; 19.7 bar a MP steam condenses on the shell. Top gas goes to the carbamate
condenser 322E002; bottom solution goes through LV-322501 to LP recirculation.

## XVIII.1 Why a calibrated split, and what "departure" means here

The split is **measured**. The licensor's heat and mass balance fixes what fraction of each
component leaves overhead at the design point, and that vector closes the plant balance to
better than 0.1 %. A rate-based column would replace that measurement with a set of
mass-transfer coefficients nobody has for this service, at this pressure, in this liquor.

So the calibration is the anchor, and every term in the model is a departure from it. Six
drivers, and each is exactly 1 (or exactly 0) at the design state:

| driver | what moves it | at design |
|---|---|---|
| $\eta_{T,steam}$ | live shell saturation temperature | $T/T_{des} = 1$ |
| $\eta_{CO_2}$ | live sweep-gas rate | $0.5 + 0.5(1) = 1$ |
| $g_T$ | steam duty spread over the live feed mass | $1 + k\cdot 0 = 1$ |
| $g_{flood}$ | the tube's hydraulic limit | $1 - 0/Q = 1$ |
| $g_{N/C},\,g_{H/C}$ | the reactor's feed ratios | $1 - k\cdot 0 = 1$ |
| $r_i$ | per-species K-value ratio at the live pressure | $K/K = 1$ |

Several of those are identities rather than tuned coincidences, which is the distinction that
matters. $g_{flood}$ is 1 because `max(0.7448 - 1.0, 0.0)` returns the **literal** 0.0 — a
one-sided constraint the plant genuinely operates below. $r_i$ is 1 because the reference
K-value is evaluated with every argument identical to the live one.

## XVIII.2 The four temperatures, and why the top and the bottom differ

$$
T_{bot} = \min\!\left(T_{bot,des} + 0.7\,\Delta T_s + \Delta T_{bot} + \Delta T_{strip},\; T_{steam}\right)
$$

$$
T_{top} = \min\!\left(T_{top,des} + 0.6\,\Delta T_s + k_{top}\,\Delta T_{bot} + \Delta T_{strip},\; T_{steam}\right)
$$

with $\Delta T_s = T_{steam} - T_{steam,des}$ and $k_{top} = 0.5$.

The asymmetry is physical, not a fit. The feed-load swing $\Delta T_{bot}$ is a **liquid-side
reboiler** effect and the rising vapour feels it only weakly, so it arrives at the overhead
attenuated. The sweep-gas flash endotherm $\Delta T_{strip}$ arrives at **full weight**,
because the rising vapour is the first thing that has to carry that latent load.

### The liquid-side energy balance

The reboiler delivers a roughly fixed duty; what the descending liquid gets is that duty
spread over the live feed mass:

$$
\text{raw} = \Delta T_{steam,des}\left(\frac{\dot m_{des}}{\dot m} - 1\right),
\qquad \Delta T_{steam,des} = \frac{Q_{des}\cdot 3600}{\dot m_{des}\,c_p} \approx 172.4\ \text{C}
$$

Open the reactor overflow valve at constant steam and each kilogram gets less heating, so the
bottom leaves **colder**. The carbamate endotherm is itself proportional to feed and cancels
its own per-mass term, which is why this steam-dilution swing is the net response.

That raw form has a pole at zero feed, so the heating branch is capped on the head-room below
the condensing shell:

$$
\Delta T_{load} = \begin{cases}
\text{cap}\left(1 - e^{-\text{raw}/\text{cap}}\right) & \text{raw} > 0 \quad\text{(low feed)}\\[2pt]
\text{raw} & \text{raw} \le 0 \quad\text{(feed spike)}
\end{cases}
$$

The high-feed branch is deliberately left as the raw negative load, because $\Delta T_{load}$
is also the **efficiency** driver: on a flood the split has to keep closing, which is what
holds the unstripped volatiles in the bottoms where they leave through LV-322501 rather than
overhead.

### Why the bottom temperature has its own driver

Feeding the raw linear load straight into the temperature drove it **down without bound** — an
infinite feed gave about $-0.4$ C, which is absurd and the wrong sign as well. The physics is
the opposite. A flooded stripper is steam-limited: carbamate decomposition stalls, its
endotherm fades, and the already-hot reactor liquor falls through the tubes untouched. So

$$
\Delta T_{bot} = \begin{cases}
\Delta T_{load} & \text{raw} > 0\\[2pt]
D\left(1 - e^{\text{raw}/D}\right) & \text{raw} \le 0
\end{cases},
\qquad D = T_{reactor} - T_{bot,des} = 11\ \text{C}
$$

and $g_T$ is left on the raw load, untouched. So a flood gives **hot but unstripped** bottoms —
which is the classic NH3 slip to the LP section, and is the lesson.

### The CO2 sweep endotherm

The compressor holds the sweep while the liquid feed varies, so a feed collapse spikes the
gas/liquid ratio. The excess gas forces carbamate decomposition and an NH3/CO2 flash, strongly
endothermic:

$$
r_{G/L} = \frac{\dot m_{CO_2}}{\dot m_{CO_2,des}}\cdot\frac{\dot m_{des}}{\dot m} - 1,
\qquad
\Delta T_{strip} = -\Delta T_{max}\left(1 - e^{-k\,\max(r_{G/L},\,0)}\right)
$$

with $\Delta T_{max} = 72$ C. This term **overpowers** the steam-heating branch: on a low-feed,
constant-CO2 excursion the bottom goes colder, not toward steam saturation. Without it the
model would teach the opposite of what happens.

## XVIII.3 The hydrodynamic flooding limit

Everything above asks whether the shell steam can keep up with the liquid. This asks the
independent question of whether the tube can carry the film at all. Once the rising gas core
shears the descending film off the wall, the film thickens, liquid is dragged upward, residence
time collapses and stripping stops however much steam is available.

**Geometry** — licensor DDS UD-AU-322-DZ-0003-003 rev 00, page 3. The DDS is self-consistent,
and that is what licenses using it for a hydraulic limit: its own tabulated exchange surface
confirms its tube count,

$$
N\pi d_o L = 2600 \times \pi \times 0.031 \times 6.000 = 1519.27\ \text{m}^2
\quad\text{vs line 25's } 1519.00 \quad (+0.018\,\%)
$$

**The limit** — Brouwer, *How to Solve Stripper Efficiency Issues*, UreaKnowHow 2025, citing
IFS Proceeding 166: at 183 C reactor outlet and 140 bar, the flooding limit in a 1-inch tube is
145 kg of solution per hour. Three facts make it applicable without adjustment: the DDS tube ID
is 25.0 mm = 0.984 inch; the DDS effective length is 6.000 m, which the same paper states is
what gives a Stamicarbon CO2 stripper its 80 % design efficiency; and the quoted reference
condition is this stripper's own feed temperature at a pressure within 3 % of its tube side.

$$
\text{flood}_{frac} = \frac{\dot m}{N\,\dot m_{tube,lim}},
\qquad \text{flood}_{frac,des} = \frac{280\,797}{2600\times 145} = 0.7448
$$

Two consequences, both load-bearing. The plant limit is 377 000 kg/h, so flooding starts at
**134 %** of design load — the same order as the paper's "110 % when new, 120 % at end of life".
And because $0.7448 < 1$ the whole block is **identically inactive** at the seed, so it cannot
move a bit of the pinned design state. That is the bit-exactness argument for it: not an
anchored ratio, just a constraint the plant operates below.

$$
\Delta T_{flood} = D\left(1 - e^{-K x}\right),\qquad x = \max(\text{flood}_{frac} - 1,\,0),\qquad K = 3.83
$$

$K$ is **fixed by the source's own observation**, not tuned: Brouwer reports a 3-4 C bottom rise
in 15 minutes as the flooding signature, and requiring $11.0\,(1 - e^{-0.10K}) = 3.5$ gives
$K = 3.83$. The model returns exactly 3.50 C at 10 % over the limit.

### The efficiency knockdown needs no constant at all

The bottom running hotter and the stripping being lost are **the same event measured two ways**:
the bottom is hot precisely because the dissociation did not happen, so the heat that should
have been absorbed shows up as sensible heat instead.

$$
g_{flood} = 1 - \frac{\dot m\, c_p\, \Delta T_{flood}}{n_{carb}\,\Delta H_{carb}}
$$

with $n_{carb}$ taken **excluding the CO2 sweep**, which arrives already gaseous and needs no
dissociation heat — so there is no circular dependence on the split this drives. Charging the
balance against the carbamate endotherm alone rather than the full endotherm sum is both the
simpler and the conservative choice (a smaller denominator gives a larger knockdown), and it is
what the source describes: it is the falling film that facilitates the dissociation.

At 10 % over the limit this gives **2.2 %**, against three independent cross-checks that all say
a few per cent rather than the 13 % a borrowed $1/(1+1.5x)$ fit had been giving:

| check | knockdown at 10 % over |
|---|---|
| this energy balance | 2.2 % |
| Brouwer's Shangdong Hualu Hengsheng case (3 C bottom rise, 79 % to 81 %) | ~2.5 % |
| the licensor length correlation (6 m eff. 80 %, 8 m eff. 82 %) on the flooded length | ~0.8 % |

`FLOOD_ETA_FLOOR = 0.50` is a guard, **not an operating state**. The feed mass cancels between
numerator and denominator, so the knockdown saturates at about 0.93 however hard the stripper is
pushed. The deep collapse belongs to $g_T$.

> **Open — handoff B-9.** $\Delta T_{bot}$ and $\Delta T_{flood}$ are each scaled on the same
> 11 C reactor-liquor gap, and both of V1's comments say they share that ceiling, but the code
> **adds** them: TT-322004 asymptotes to 194 C, not 183. The two always co-activate, because
> both are functions of the same feed mass. Reproduced rather than corrected; the decision is
> the process engineer's.

## XVIII.4 The split, and the two ways the composition penalty does NOT act

$$
\text{mod} = \operatorname{clamp}(\eta_{T,steam}\,\eta_{CO_2},\,0,\,1.12)\cdot\min(g_T,1)\cdot g_{flood}
$$

$$
\theta_i = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\Phi\big(\alpha_{i,PFD}\cdot\text{mod},\; r_i\big),\; 0,\; 0.999\right),
\qquad
\Phi(\theta, r) = \frac{r\theta}{1 + (r-1)\theta}
$$

$\Phi$ is the fixed-phase-ratio transform of Part XV: back-solve $K$ from
$\theta = K\psi/(1+\psi(K-1))$, re-insert $Kr$, and the $(1-\psi)$ factors cancel so $\psi$ drops
out entirely. A stripper is not a flash — nothing fixes its vapour fraction — so inventing one
in order to move a calibrated split would be inventing physics.

Two properties, both structural. $\Phi$ maps $[0,1]$ onto $[0,1]$ for any $r>0$, which the bare
`theta * eta_P` multiply it replaced could not: at $\eta_P = 1.15$ the N2 split went to 1.148
before a clamp silently truncated it — the column was being asked to strip more nitrogen than
entered it. And $(r-1)$ is exactly 0.0 at $r=1$, so $\Phi$ returns $\theta$ to the last bit by
the arithmetic rather than by a short-circuit.

**Only the pressure moves in $r_i$.** The thermal response of the split is already carried, and
carried better, by $\eta_{T,steam}$: the stripper is a steam-driven contactor, not an adiabatic
flash, and its bottoms temperature is an *output* of that duty. Putting the live temperature
into the ratio as well would count the same steam heat twice, so the reference temperature IS
the live temperature and the two K-values' temperature terms cancel identically.

### Slip: what the composition penalty actually does

$$
g_{N/C} = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(1 - k_N(L - L_0),\,0.5,\,1.05\right),
\qquad
g_{H/C} = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(1 - k_W(W - W_0),\,0.5,\,1.05\right)
$$

$$
\text{slip} = \max(1-g_{N/C},0) + \max(1-g_{H/C},0),
\qquad
\theta_i \leftarrow \theta_i + G\,\text{slip}\,(1 - \theta_i) \quad i \in \{NH_3, CO_2\}
$$

This is the counter-intuitive part, and it is why the penalty is not a multiplier on the split.
A solution that is hard to strip **thermally** does not quietly keep its volatiles: it breaks
them through to the overhead, and the carbamate condenser downstream has to take them. So the
*reported* efficiency falls while *more* NH3 and CO2 leave the top.

$L_0$ and $W_0$ are the **reactor's** design feed ratios, not this unit's own. That is a
modelling constraint rather than a preference: the reduced reactor pins its overflow N/C
through an atom-conserving ripple, so the stripper's own feed ratio barely moves and would
carry no disturbance, while the reactor-feed ratios are the ones that actually drop conversion
and load this stripper. They arrive one tick old, as a declared tear.

## XVIII.5 The two reactions, and why one is anchored

**Urea hydrolysis**, $\mathrm{NH_2CONH_2 + H_2O \rightarrow 2\,NH_3 + CO_2}$, on Inoue & Otsuka
(1973) Eq. (6), $\ln k_H = 21.8 - 11100/T$ — the same law 328C003 runs on, and now a shared
property in `thermo/kinetics.py` rather than two copies:

$$
\xi_{hyd} = \xi_{hyd,des}\cdot\frac{k(T_{bot})\,C_U\,C_W\,V_{liq}}{\left[k\,C_U\,C_W\,V_{liq}\right]_{des}},
\qquad C_i = \frac{\dot n_i}{\dot V}
$$

**Why the extent is anchored and not predicted.** This was measured, not assumed. At the
stripper's own design state the rate group returns

| holdup | group |
|---|---|
| tube bundle only, 7.658 m3 | 12.02 kmol/h |
| bundle + sump at its design level, 11.136 m3 | 17.48 kmol/h |
| the whole vessel liquid-full, 14.615 m3 | 22.94 kmol/h |
| **the PFD extent** | **88.10 kmol/h** |

Even liquid-full the law reaches 26 % of it, and 88.1 kmol/h is 6.8 % of the urea feed destroyed
in 97 seconds where a real CO2 stripper loses well under 1 %. The PFD constant is therefore
**not urea hydrolysis alone** — it almost certainly lumps carbamate decomposition, which is what
the stripper is for. Predicting it from a hydrolysis rate law would be fitting a rate constant to
a different reaction. So the licensor extent stays the anchor and the rate law supplies the
departure: how the extent moves with temperature, concentration and holdup. That departure is the
part that was previously wrong — it used to be $\xi_{hyd,des}\cdot\eta_T$, a product of
fabricated ratio penalties with no rate constant, no residence time and no water concentration
anywhere in it.

**Biuret formation**, $\mathrm{2\,Urea \rightarrow Biuret + NH_3}$:

$$
\xi_{biu} = \xi_{biu,des}\,
\exp\!\left[\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_{des}} - \frac{1}{T_{bot}}\right)\right]
\left(\frac{\dot n_U}{\dot n_{U,des}}\right)^{2}
\frac{\dot V_{des}}{\dot V}\,\frac{V_{liq}}{V_{liq,des}}
$$

**Second** order, because that is the stoichiometry — the superseded form was first order in a
bare feed ratio — and integrated over the live liquid volume, which the superseded form had not
at all. $V_{liq}$ tracks the live LT-322501 level, so the holdup is a real state.

A consequence worth stating because it is easy to get backwards: a *proportional* turndown does
not raise biuret per unit of urea, because concentration and residence time move together and
cancel. What raises it is holding liquid up while throughput falls — the sump level, not the
feed rate — and a hotter bottom through the Arrhenius term.

Both extents are bounded by what is actually present: $\xi_{hyd} \le \min(\dot n_U, \dot n_W)$
and $\xi_{biu} \le \tfrac12(\dot n_U - \xi_{hyd})$.

## XVIII.6 What the MP-steam header actually pays for

The superseded form was duty proportional to feed **mass**, which says a stripper fed the same
tonnage of pure water and of carbamate-rich reactor liquor needs the same steam. Composition did
not enter at all, so the largest heat sink in the unit was invisible to the steam header.

$$
Q_{raw} = \underbrace{n_{CO_2}^{des}\Delta H_{carb}}_{\sim 58\,\%}
+ \underbrace{n_{NH_3}^{free}\Delta H_{NH_3}}_{}
+ \underbrace{n_{H_2O}^{top}\lambda_{H_2O}}_{\sim 7\,\%}
+ \underbrace{\xi_{hyd}\Delta H_{hyd}}_{<0}
+ \underbrace{\left[\dot m_{bot}c_{p,l} + \dot m_{top}c_{p,g}\right]\!(T - T_{feed})}_{\text{sensible}}
$$

Every constant is sourced. Frejacques, quoted in Brouwer, *Thermodynamics of the Urea Process*
(2009) p.12, gives both reactions at **process** conditions rather than at 25 C standard state:
$\mathrm{CO_2(g) + 2NH_3(g) \rightarrow NH_2COONH_4(l)}$ at $-117$ kJ/mol (110 atm, 160 C), and
$\mathrm{NH_2COONH_4(l) \rightarrow urea(l) + H_2O(l)}$ at $+15.5$ kJ/mol (160-180 C). Those
conditions are close to this stripper's own, which is why 117 is used and not the 159-160 kJ/mol
quoted for *solid* carbamate at 1 atm. The stripper runs reaction 1 backwards, so $+117$ kJ per
mol of CO2 released; hydrolysis runs reaction 2 backwards, so $-15.5$.

NH3 is **supercritical** at stripper temperature ($T_c = 132.4$ C), so there is no latent heat to
look up; what the duty pays is the desorption enthalpy out of the melt, 23 kJ/mol — the same
value the loop already uses at the other end of the same circuit.

Each term subtracts the **CO2 sweep**, which arrives already hot and already gaseous and is not
something this unit pays to liberate. The NH3 pairing is 2:1, the carbamate stoichiometry.

**Validation, and how the residue is handled.** Summed over the design streams with nothing
fitted, this gives **37 831 kW** against the licensor's 39 400 kW — 96.0 %. The 4 % residue is
shell and ambient loss, biuret (unpublished enthalpy, and 0.667 kmol/h against 88.1), and the
mean-$c_p$ approximation. That agreement is the corroboration that the constant set is right.

The absolute number is then **never used**. Only the ratio reaches the steam header:

$$
Q_{strip} = Q_{des}\cdot\frac{Q_{raw}(\text{live})}{Q_{raw}(\text{design})}\cdot 3600
$$

Both are produced by the same function from the same inputs at design, so the ratio is exactly
$X/X = 1.0$, the 4 % offset cancels, and the duty the plant is scheduled on stays the PFD value
rather than a computed one.

## XVIII.7 Design closure, and where the section ends

At the design state the two implementations agree on all 46 published fields to the bit, and the
licensor's own numbers come back exactly: TT-322004 at 172.0 C, TT-322013 at 187.0 C,
$\xi_{hyd} = 88.1$, $\xi_{biu} = 0.667$, $\eta_T = 1.0$, bottoms 130 480 kg/h against the PFD's
130 482, and every one of the six drivers a literal 1.0 or 0.0.

The unit ends at two streams and a duty: the top gas to 322E002, the bottom solution to
LV-322501, and $Q_{raw}$ to the 329D005 steam draw. The sump that holds that bottom solution —
LT-322501, LIC-322501, LV-322501, the bottoms transit lag and the sump energy balance — is
dynamics rather than a split, and is a separate module.

Three anchors leave this unit for the rest of the loop, and all three are computed by evaluating
the model at its own design point rather than entered as literals: the design overhead vector
(5789.40 kmol/h total, 3571.60 of it NH3), the **free CO2** overhead (98.60 kmol/h, the CO2 not
paired into carbamate at 2 NH3 per CO2 — the acid that actually pushes PT-329201 up, since
carbamate condenses and takes its partial pressure with it), and the design enthalpy balance.
