# Part XIX — Deviation-consequence physics: the lost liquid seal and the mushy zone

Two relations in this simulator do not belong to any one piece of equipment. They describe what
happens to ANY level-controlled vessel when it runs dry, and to ANY urea-bearing line when it
cools, and they are called from several units. They are collected in
`ureasim/units/consequence/`.

## XIX.0 Why they are generic, and what that fixed

In V1 every written-up deviation scenario was wired in at the one tag it had been written up
against, with its own hand-picked constant. Losing the liquid seal on 323C003 and losing it on
328C004 are the same event — a drain nozzle uncovers and the vessel's gas inventory escapes
through a valve sized for liquid — and one of them produced 5000 kg/h of gas while the other
produced nothing at all, because nobody had written that scenario down yet. A trainee who learns
the plant on a model like that learns the model's authoring history.

Three properties are required of every relation in this part, and both of the ported ones have
all three:

1. **It returns exactly the null effect at the design state.** Not approximately. The whole
   flowsheet is pinned at the 1750 MTPD design point and a settled boot captures calibration
   constants from that fixed point, so a consequence that contributed $10^{-14}$ at design would
   contaminate the pin.
2. **It is continuous in its arguments.** `if level <= 0` is a step change in the right-hand
   side of a level ODE. It chatters, and it cannot be undone by correct operator action.
3. **It enters as a RATE that an existing balance integrates.** Never as a state override. A
   vessel pressure ASSIGNED 1.013 bar a cannot recover; one DRIVEN toward 1.013 bar a by an
   ingress rate can.

## XIX.1 The liquid seal over a drain nozzle

A drain nozzle does not uncover at a mathematical point. It uncovers over its own bore, and
across that band the valve passes a two-phase mixture whose gas fraction grows with the
uncovered area:

$$ \sigma \;=\; \mathrm{clamp}\!\left(\frac{L - L_{seal}}{\Delta L_{band}},\; 0,\; 1\right) $$

with $\sigma = 1$ fully sealed and $\sigma = 0$ fully open to the vapour space. $L_{seal}$ is
the transmitter reading at which the nozzle is just fully uncovered — the nozzle centreline —
and $\Delta L_{band}$ is the bore in the same per-cent-of-span units, generically 3 %.

Writing it as a ramp does three things at once, and each of them matters on the plant:

* it removes the step from every level ODE;
* it reproduces the real behaviour that blow-through **starts before the transmitter reads
  zero**, because on most of these vessels the level tap sits above the drain nozzle;
* it makes the transition reversible, so restoring level restores the seal.

Every consequence keyed on a lost seal is written as $(1 - \sigma)$, so all of them are exactly
zero whenever the vessel holds a normal level.

**Limiter.** This one preserves a NaN rather than pinning it to the upper bound. A NaN level
that came back as "fully sealed" would report a healthy drain, which is the one failure mode
the relation exists to catch.

## XIX.2 What the same trim passes as gas

A control valve's flow coefficient is a property of the VALVE, not of the fluid, so it can be
eliminated between the liquid duty it was sized on and the compressible flow it is now passing.
From the liquid design duty,

$$ C \;=\; \frac{\dot m_{liq,des}}{N\sqrt{\rho_{liq}\,\Delta P_{des}}} $$

and from IEC 60534-2-1 compressible flow at a stroke $\theta$,

$$ \dot m_{gas} \;=\; N\,C\,\theta\,Y\sqrt{\rho_{gas}\,\Delta P_{eff}} $$

$N$ and $C$ cancel identically, leaving the form this simulator uses:

$$ \boxed{\;\dot m_{gas} \;=\; \dot m_{liq,des}\;\theta\;Y\;
\sqrt{\frac{\rho_{gas}\,\Delta P_{eff}}{\rho_{liq}\,\Delta P_{des}}}\;(1-\sigma)\;} $$

The expansion factor and the choke come from the same standard:

$$ x = \frac{\Delta P}{P_1},\qquad
   F_k = \frac{\gamma}{1.40},\qquad
   x_{ch} = F_k\,x_T,\qquad
   x_{eff} = \min(x,\,x_{ch}) $$

$$ Y = \mathrm{clamp}\!\left(1 - \frac{x_{eff}}{3\,x_{ch}},\; \tfrac23,\; 1\right),
   \qquad \Delta P_{eff} = x_{eff}\,P_1 $$

with $x_T = 0.70$ for a generic single-seat globe trim and $\gamma = 1.30$ for the NH3 / CO2 /
H2O vapours in this plant. $Y$ runs from 1 at a vanishing drop to exactly $2/3$ at the choke
point; the 1.40 in $F_k$ is air, the reference gas the $x_T$ tables are measured on.

**Why the choke is the important half.** Past $x_{ch}$ the vena contracta is sonic and the mass
flow stops responding to the downstream side entirely. That is why a seal-loss blow-through has
a CEILING instead of running away as the downstream section depressurises, and it is the
difference between a trainable upset and a numerical explosion in the downstream pressure node.
Note what it does NOT remove: the upstream side. A blow-through still scales with $P_1$, and
roughly linearly, because $\Delta P_{eff}$ and $\rho_{gas}$ are both proportional to it.

**Magnitudes, and why the derivation was worth doing.** At LV-322501's design stroke and design
loop pressure with the nozzle fully uncovered, the relation gives **25.4 t/h** of stripper
vapour into the LP section, against a **25 t/h** that had been hand-entered for that one valve
in V1. The hand number was the right order and was defensible where it stood; what it could not
do was transfer to any other valve, which is the entire argument for the derivation.

The $\sqrt{\rho_{gas}/\rho_{liq}}$ factor is the physical story an operator needs, and it has
two halves that point in opposite directions. In MASS the valve passes far less than its liquid
duty. In VOLUME — which is what the receiving vessel feels — the ratio is
$Y\sqrt{\rho_{liq}/\rho_{gas}}$ at a matched differential, so it depends on how dense the
vapour is:

| valve | $P_1$ | $\rho_{gas}$ | volumetric ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| LV-322501, stripper sump | 140.7 bar a | 144 kg/m3 | about 1.5 |
| LV-323501, 323C003 drain | 4.2 bar a | 2.6 kg/m3 | about 16 |

which is why the same event is far more violent for the LP section than for the HP one.

**Real-gas correction.** The relation takes $\rho_{gas}$ as an argument rather than computing
it, and `gas_density_ideal` is ideal gas by design. Where a node is dense enough for that to
matter the caller divides by a compressibility factor from `thermo.real_gas` — at LV-322501,
$Z = 0.685$ at 140.7 bar a and 172 C, so the true density is **1.46 times** the ideal-gas value
and the blow-through rate is 21 % higher than an ideal-gas calculation would give. Keeping the
equation of state in the thermo layer is what stops an SRK call from being buried inside a
consequence helper.

## XIX.3 The mushy zone

A urea melt and a carbamate liquor both salt out as they cool, and neither does it at a point.
Between the first crystals and a solid stream there is a slurry whose apparent viscosity climbs
until the line no longer flows:

$$ f \;=\; \mathrm{clamp}\!\left(\frac{T - T_{cryst}}{\Delta T_{mush}},\; 0,\; 1\right),
   \qquad \Delta T_{mush} = 5\ \text{C} $$

Two boundaries are used in this flowsheet: 132.7 C, the pure-urea melting point, at the 322E001
bottoms; and 60.0 C, the carbamate boundary, at the 322E003 scrubber overflow.

**Why a factor and not a trip.** Plugging is progressive and recoverable, and a trainee has to
be able to watch it happen and reverse it. The un-drained mass stays in the vessel's own level
ODE, so the LEVEL RISES while the drain falls — which is the signature an operator actually
gets, minutes before anything stops moving. A threshold would give them a working line and then
a dead one.

**Limiter.** This one takes the engine limiter, so a non-finite temperature returns 1.0 — an
unrestricted line. That is stated rather than defended: it is V1's behaviour at every reachable
call site and §5 of the agent directives forbids improving it during the port. V1's
`consequence.py` holds a second copy of the same relation that preserves a NaN instead, and
nothing calls it.

## XIX.4 What is in V1 and is deliberately not here

`backend/consequence.py` is 640 lines and only three of its functions are ever called from the
engine. A Souders-Brown carry-over departure, an NPSH margin knee, a urea and ammonium carbamate
solubility curve, a choked air-ingress orifice and a one-call vessel block are all written and
all unreferenced. They are better physics than what some of the units they were meant for
currently contain, and they should return with the unit that needs one — at which point each
gets a call site and a test. What must not happen is 500 lines of untestable generic physics
entering the rewrite because it existed in V1. `handoff.md` and the Session 8 log in
`project.md` carry the count.

---

# Part XX — Unit 322E001 (continued): the bottom sump, LIC-322501 and LV-322501

Part XVIII ends at two streams and a duty. This part is what happens to the bottom one. Below
the falling-film tubes, 322E001 has a bottom head that is a buffer, a level measurement and a
thermal residence volume at once, and everything the stripper makes leaves the synthesis loop
through the one valve underneath it — a letdown from 140 bar a to 4 bar a, the largest single
pressure drop on the plant.

The sump is a separate module from the bundle because it is a separate kind of object. The
bundle is a pure function: the same feed and the same steam give the same answer every time. The
sump integrates — it has a level, a controller with a memory and a transport line with a FIFO in
it. The level feeds back into the bundle through the liquid holdup the two reaction rate laws
see, and that is a declared tear: the bundle is evaluated with the level from the top of the
tick.

## XX.1 LIC-322501, and why it is a third controller form

$$ \Delta u \;=\; K_c\Big[(e_k - e_{k-1}) + \frac{\Delta t}{T_i}e_k\Big],
   \qquad e = PV - SP,
   \qquad OP = \mathrm{clamp}(OP + \Delta u,\, 0,\, 100) $$

with $K_c = 2.5$ and $T_i = 90$ s. Direct acting on a fail-closed, air-to-open valve, which is
correct negative feedback: the level rises, the output rises, LV-322501 opens, the drain rises,
the level comes back. On a trip the air fails and the valve shuts, keeping the loop's inventory
inside the loop.

**Proportional-dominant, and that is not a preference.** A level is an INTEGRATING process — the
valve sets a flow and a flow accumulates into a level. An integral-dominant controller on an
integrating process is two integrators in series, and the loop limit-cycles.

**Why it is not `control.process_loop.ProcessLoop`.** Because the proportional term acts on the
ERROR, not on the PV. With a constant set point the two are the same expression: $e_k - e_{k-1}$
reduces to $PV_k - PV_{k-1}$ and the whole thing is a direct-acting I-PD. They separate the
moment an operator moves the set point, where this form gives a proportional kick out of the
valve of $-K_c\,\Delta SP$ and the I-PD form gives none. That kick is real DCS behaviour for
this configuration and it is part of what a trainee is being taught. LIC-322501 is the only loop
in V1 written this way, so the form stays local to this module rather than becoming a generic
class.

**Bad-PV handling, and a contrast worth recording.** On a non-finite level or set point this
loop holds the last good error and skips the increment, so `e_prev` is re-assigned its own value
and the output is genuinely frozen. That is what "freeze last good" means and it is implemented
correctly here. V1's inline PIC-322203 carries the same comment and does NOT do it; the rewrite
installs that loop as a `ProcessLoop`, by decision (§XVII.5), so both loops now freeze.

## XX.2 The letdown law

$$ \dot m_{drain} \;=\; \dot m_{des}\;\frac{Op}{Op_{des}}\;
   \sqrt{\frac{\max(P_{syn} - P_{down},\,0)}{\Delta P_{des}}} $$

Linear in the stroke because the trim is linear; square-root in the head because that is
incompressible flow through a fixed resistance. Both ratios are exactly 1.0 at design, so the
PFD bottoms flow of 130 482 kg/h comes back bit-exact.

**Why the LIVE loop pressure (finding L3-1).** LV-322501 is a pressure letdown, not a gravity
drain. What pushes liquor through it is the loop's own pressure, so on a black start with the
loop at atmospheric the valve can be wide open and pass nothing. A frozen design differential
would have the sump draining itself into an unpressurised LP section every time. $P_{syn}$ is
PT-329201 read from the previous tick — the same loop-break convention the rest of the HP loop
uses.

**Which differential (handoff A-13).** $\Delta P_{des}$ here is 136.7 bar, and it is derived as
$P_{syn,des} - P_{down} = 140.7 - 4.0$. It is NOT the valve datasheet's 139.8 bar, which is
measured between the 144.0 bar a shell and the 4.2 bar a line downstream of the valve. Both
numbers are real, both are subtractions, and both are about the same valve — but only the first
is measured between the two pressures this law's live arguments are read from, and only the
first therefore gives a ratio of exactly 1.0 at design. Substituting one for the other moves the
blow-through by 1.1 % while leaving every design-point assertion passing.

## XX.3 The two restrictions, in the order they apply

$$ \dot m_{drain} \;\leftarrow\; \dot m_{drain}\;\cdot\;f(T_{bot},\,132.7)\;\cdot\;\sigma(L) $$

The mushy-zone factor comes from Part XIX.3 and the seal from XIX.1. Both multiply the LIQUID
drain, and the order between them does not matter because they commute — but the order relative
to the mass balance does, and it is the point of the whole arrangement: the restricted drain is
what enters the level ODE, so mass that does not leave stays in the vessel.

**The closing-direction runaway.** This is the operating lesson the sump exists to teach, and
it is emergent rather than scripted:

| $T_{bot}$ | $f$ | LIC-322501 output | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 172 C | 1.00 | 46.1 % | design |
| 136 C | 0.66 | 53.8 % (V1: about 70 %) | recovered — the loop simply strokes further open |
| 134 C | 0.26 | 100 %, railed | sump floods to 100 %, drain 74 % of design (V1: below 60 %) |

The colder bottoms boil lower and LV-322501's flashing choke relaxes (B-46, §XLIV.2): the
restriction is met with less stroke, and the rail passes more

Between the second row and the third the operator loses the loop. What they see beforehand is a
valve position that has drifted far from normal at an apparently normal flow, which is the cue.

**Blow-through, and why AUTO suppresses it (finding D-20).** Once the outlet nozzle uncovers the
valve keeps flowing and starts passing the stripper's own vapour, per XIX.2, at the stripper's
own composition and the sump temperature with the SRK correction applied. But emptying this sump
in AUTO drives LIC-322501's output to zero within a tick or two, so the valve shuts before the
nozzle is uncovered. **Blow-through here is a manual-mode or a saturation event** — which is
correct, and is also when it is most likely to happen on the plant.

## XX.4 The bottoms transit (finding D-8)

$$ t_d \;=\; \mathrm{clamp}\!\left(\frac{\rho\,V_{line}}{\dot m}\cdot 3600,\; 0,\; 3600\right),
   \qquad V_{line} = \frac{\dot m_{des}\,t_{d,des}}{3600\,\rho} = 1.917\ \text{m}^3 $$

V1 carried a flat 60 s FIFO here, labelled empirical and motionless from turndown to trip. The
60 s is kept as the DESIGN transit, the line inventory is back-solved from it at the design
flow, and the live dead time is $\rho V/\dot m$ — so a stripper at half rate takes 120 s to
deliver its bottoms to the sump, which is what actually happens. Capped at 3600 s so a stalled
line gives a long-but-finite delay rather than an unbounded buffer.

## XX.5 The LT-322501 mass balance (finding A-3)

$$ L_{k+1} \;=\; \mathrm{clamp}\!\left(L_k +
   \frac{\dot m_{in}(t - t_d) - \dot m_{drain}}{3600}\cdot
   \frac{\Delta t}{A\,H\,\rho}\cdot 100,\; 0,\; 100\right) $$

with $A = 4.638$ m2, $H = 1.5$ m and $\rho = 1134.64$ kg/m3, giving a span of 7893 kg.

Two things were removed from V1 to get here, and both were removals rather than changes. The
**fill gate** — a Smith-fitted $k = 0.06 + 0.94\,m_{loop}^8$ that multiplied every net inflow —
deleted 94 % of the net flow at low loop inventory, which is to say it deleted mass; at design
$k$ was exactly 1, so removing it leaves the design seed untouched and makes the cold-start fill
time an emergent property. The **empty-sump guard** that clipped the drain to the inflow is gone
because the seal ramp now takes the liquid to zero as the level reaches the nozzle, and what the
valve passes past that point is gas.

**A 2 kg/h imbalance at design, and it is real.** The bundle's split gives 130 480 kg/h and the
letdown law is normalised on the PFD's 130 482 kg/h. Two numbers from two places in the same
licensor package, agreeing to 15 ppm. With the loop in MAN the level therefore falls at 0.025 %
per hour; in AUTO the loop absorbs it with a 0.001 % stroke change and it is unobservable. It is
recorded rather than reconciled, because reconciling it would mean choosing which of the two
licensor numbers to overwrite.

## XX.6 The sump energy balance (finding L3-7)

The sump is a stirred buffer that loses heat, and how much it loses depends on how long the
liquor sits in it — which depends on how far LV-322501 is open. Steady state:

$$ \dot m\,c_p\,T_{film} \;=\; \dot m\,c_p\,T_{out} + UA\,(T_{out} - T_{amb}) $$

Part XVIII's $T_{bot}$ is already the DESIGN-drain sump outlet, because that is what the
licensor balance is anchored on, so the film above it is
$T_{film} = T_{bot}(1+\tau) - \tau T_{amb}$ with $\tau = UA/(\dot m_{des}c_p)$. Eliminating the
film and writing $r = \dot m_{drain}/\dot m_{des}$ gives the closed form:

$$ \boxed{\;T_{out} \;=\;
   \frac{r(1+\tau)\,T_{bot} \;+\; \tau(1-r)\,T_{amb}}{r + \tau}\;}
   \qquad \tau = \frac{\Delta T_{loss,des}}{T_{bot,des} - T_{cryst}} = 0.10178 $$

**Everything about this form is anchored or structural, and nothing in it is tuned.**

* At $r = 1$ it returns $T_{bot}$ **exactly**, so the design heat and mass balance is untouched.
* Its derivative is $\tau(1+\tau)(T_{bot} - T_{amb})/(r+\tau)^2$, which is positive whenever the
  bottoms are above the floor. The sign is therefore guaranteed rather than fitted: **more drain
  is always hotter**. Opening LV-322501 does not only move more product, it moves hotter
  product, because there is less residence time in which to lose heat.
* As $r \to \infty$ it approaches $T_{film} = 176.0$ C, the temperature of the liquor actually
  leaving the tubes.
* As $r \to 0$ it approaches $T_{amb}$, which here is the 132.7 C crystallisation floor rather
  than a plant ambient. That is deliberate: it is the temperature a throttled sump asymptotes
  to, and the temperature at which the consequence of getting there occurs. **This is what
  closes the loop with XX.3** — throttling cools the bottoms, cooling throttles them further.
* Capped at the condensing shell, because a bottoms stream cannot out-heat the steam that heats
  it. Unlike some of the guards in Part XVIII this one is reachable: it binds above about 205 C
  of film feed.
* Below the crystallisation floor the relation is bypassed entirely and the film temperature
  passes straight through. On a cold start there is no hot-film residence effect to model, and
  the closed form would be extrapolating a heat loss against a temperature difference of the
  wrong sign.

$T_{out}$ reaches the operator through the stripper's own thermal time constant — 180 s of
falling-film and sump liquid holdup plus HP shell metal, process inertia rather than transmitter
damping — and the 323C003 inlet temperature follows it at an anchored gain:

$$ TT\text{-}323001 \;=\; 119.0 + 0.7\,(T_{out} - 172.0) $$

exactly 119.0 C at design. The 0.7 is the fraction of a bottoms-temperature swing that survives
the letdown flash: a hotter feed flashes off more vapour, and the extra latent load pulls the
remaining liquid back toward the same saturation temperature.

## XX.7 Where the published temperature goes, and where it does not

$TT\text{-}322004$ is the one value this sump publishes that another SECTION reads: the 323C003
letdown-flash duty is sized on it. In V1 it never arrives. The lag writes into the tear store
under the key `"TT322004"` and the 323 block reads `"TT_322004"`, which is never written, so the
`.get` default fires on every tick and the flash duty has been running on a constant 172.0 C.
The flash gas leaving 323C003 therefore does not respond to how hot the stripper bottoms
actually are, although the sign of the suppressed term is unambiguous — it enters linearly and
positively.

This was handoff **B-10**: a recycle tear whose source never publishes. **Decided
2026-09-26 and closed with the 323C003 port: the column reads the live value** (§XXVIII.6).
At the design state this sump publishes exactly 172.0 C, so the 323C003 calibration point is
not moved; only the column's response to a stripper running hot or cold is.

## XX.8 Design closure

At the design state every anchored quantity returns its PFD value and four of them return it
exactly: the drain at 130 482 kg/h, the sump outlet at 172.0 C, TT-323001 at 119.0 C, the seal
at 1.0 and the blow-through at 0.0 — the last by RETURN rather than by arithmetic, through the
`seal >= 1.0` short circuit. The mushy-zone factor is 1.0 and the transit is 60.0 s.

Unit 322E001 is complete.

# Part XXI — The liquid-liquid jet pump: a constant-area closure with one root

A jet pump has no moving parts and therefore no free parameters. A motive liquid is
accelerated through a nozzle, the jet entrains a second liquid, the two mix in a constant-area
throat and a diffuser recovers pressure. The machine's entire characteristic follows from four
balances. This part is those balances; Part XXII is the plant they are attached to.

## XXI.0 What this replaced, and why it is a different kind of model

V1's engine computed the entrainment as

$$ \text{capacity} = \dot m_{suc,des}\,\phi_m\,\phi_{sp}\,f_{stall},
   \qquad f_{stall} = \mathrm{clamp}\!\left(\frac{\phi_m - 0.20}{0.35 - 0.20},0,1\right)^{2} $$

Every part of that is a curve fitted to the desired behaviour rather than a statement about
the machine:

* the entrainment RATIO is asserted constant across the healthy band;
* the collapse on a motive fault is a polynomial with three fitted constants and no physical
  meaning;
* the spindle acts on the ANSWER, through an equal-percentage factor, instead of on the
  nozzle area where a needle actually acts.

The directions were all right. Nothing in it could be wrong in an interesting way, because
nothing in it was derived. With the momentum balance in place all three become consequences,
and two of them come out different enough to be findings — see XXII.3 and XXII.4.

## XXI.1 The four balances

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{nozzle} \quad & V_p = \frac{\dot m_p}{\rho_p A_t} \\[2pt]
\text{suction inlet} \quad & p_1 = p_s - (1 + K_{en})\frac{\dot m_s^2}{2\rho_s A_s^2} \\[2pt]
\text{throat momentum} \quad & (p_2 - p_1)A_m = \dot m_p V_p + \dot m_s V_s - \dot m_m V_m
   - K_{th}\frac{\dot m_m^2}{2\rho_m A_m} \\[2pt]
\text{diffuser} \quad & p_d = p_2 + \eta_d \frac{\dot m_m^2}{2\rho_m A_m^2}
\end{aligned}
$$

with $A_s = A_m - A_t$ and $\dot m_m = \dot m_p + \dot m_s$. The motive mass flow is set by
the positive-displacement pumps upstream, so the nozzle AREA is what fixes the jet velocity —
not the other way round, and that is the whole reason the spindle law runs backwards.

Collected, the pressure rise is a quadratic in the entrained flow:

$$ p_d - p_s = C_0 + C_1 \dot m_s + C_2 \dot m_s^2 $$

$$
\begin{aligned}
B &= \frac{-1 - \tfrac12 K_{th} + \tfrac12\eta_d}{\rho_m A_m^2} \;<\; 0 \\
A &= \frac{1}{\rho_s A_s A_m} - \frac{1 + K_{en}}{2\rho_s A_s^2} \\
C_0 &= \frac{\dot m_p^2}{\rho_p A_t A_m} + B\,\dot m_p^2 ,\qquad
C_1 = 2B\,\dot m_p ,\qquad
C_2 = A + B
\end{aligned}
$$

$C_0$ is the SHUTOFF HEAD: what the jet develops when it entrains nothing. It is the ceiling
on what the machine can lift, and everything in XXII.4 follows from how close the design lift
sits to it.

## XXI.2 Why it has one root, and why that had to be proved

An earlier incompressible attempt was abandoned because it was BISTABLE. Its $\dot m_s^2$
coefficient was

$$ \frac{1}{\rho_s A_s A_m} - \frac{0.625}{\rho_m A_m^2} $$

which is net POSITIVE for any sensible area ratio — so the recovered pressure eventually RISES
with entrainment, the closure has two roots, and the characteristic degenerates to a step.

The missing term is the SUCTION-INLET ACCELERATION. The entrained stream does not arrive at
the throat entry plane at rest; it has been accelerated to $V_s = \dot m_s/(\rho_s A_s)$, and
that costs a velocity head $-(1+K_{en})\dot m_s^2/(2\rho_s A_s^2)$. It enters with $1/A_s^2$
where the cross term enters with $1/(A_s A_m)$, and since $A_s < A_m$ the missing term is the
LARGER of the two. Restoring it flips the sign of the group.

That is not a tuning, because the resulting condition is checkable. The positive part of $A$
is largest as $A_s \to A_m$, where it is $(1-K_{en})/(2\rho_s A_m^2)$, and $|B|$ is at least
$(2 + K_{th} - \eta_d)/(2\rho_m A_m^2)$. So $C_2 \le 0$ at EVERY area ratio whenever

$$ \boxed{\;\frac{\rho_m}{\rho_s} \;\le\; \frac{2 + K_{th} - \eta_d}{1 - K_{en}}\;} $$

At the 322F001 anchors — $\rho_m$ 877.9, $\rho_s$ 1133.0, $K_{th}$ 0.05, $\eta_d$ 0.80,
$K_{en}$ 0.10 — the left side is 0.775 against 1.25 on the right, a margin of **1.792**.
`monotonicity_margin` returns that ratio and `data/unit_322f001.py` ASSERTS it is above 1 at
import, so a future change to either density that would re-open the degeneracy fails loudly
instead of shipping a step characteristic.

With $C_2 \le 0$ and $C_1 < 0$ the parabola's vertex lies at negative $\dot m_s$, the
discharge is strictly decreasing on $\dot m_s \ge 0$, and there is exactly one non-negative
root — in closed form, with no iteration and nothing to converge to the wrong branch.

## XXI.3 The two hard bounds

$$ \dot m_s = \frac{-C_1 - \sqrt{C_1^2 - 4C_2(C_0 - \Delta P)}}{2C_2} $$

**Stall**, when $C_0 \le \Delta P$: the jet cannot develop the required lift even at zero
entrainment, and the entrainment is then exactly zero. This is the physical statement the
$f_{stall}$ polynomial was standing in for, and it arrives with no knee, no recovery fraction
and no convexity exponent. A jet pump that cannot lift its own discharge entrains NOTHING; it
does not entrain backwards. Reverse flow through the suction is a different flow path and
would need its own model, not a sign flip.

**Cavitation**, when the throat-entry static pressure reaches the suction fluid's vapour
pressure. From the suction-inlet balance, $p_1 \ge p_v$ caps the entrainment at

$$ \dot m_{s,max} = \rho_s A_s \sqrt{\frac{2(p_s - p_v)}{\rho_s (1 + K_{en})}} $$

Both flags are returned rather than folded into the flow, because which bound is active is a
different plant event from merely running off design.

$p_v$ is left at zero on 322F001, which degrades the bound to the absolute-pressure floor — a
static pressure cannot go negative. That is still a strict thermodynamic bound, and it is the
one that applies when the available NPSH is not known from a source. It is not known here: the
seal-leg height is in no document in the reference archive, the same blocker the handoff
records for 323F010's barometric leg. The consequence is that on this machine the cavitation
ceiling binds only below about 0.2 bar a of suction, so at 140 bar a it is a guard rather than
an operating state.

## XXI.4 The geometry back-solve

`References/Datasheets/322F001 Design Calculations.pdf` is a 12-page scan with no text layer,
so the two areas cannot be read out of the archive. They are derived from the licensor's own
duty through the same equations the model runs forward — the identical treatment every control
valve in this engine gets, and for the identical reason: it keeps the design point exact and
it invents nothing.

Two equations, two unknowns. The nozzle passes the design motive flow at the design nozzle
differential,

$$ V_p = \sqrt{\frac{2(p_{mot} - p_1)}{\rho_p (1 + K_n)}},
   \qquad A_t = \frac{\dot m_p}{\rho_p V_p} $$

and the closure develops exactly the design discharge rise at the design entrainment. $A_t$
and $p_1$ depend on each other, so the inner solve is a fixed point; it converges in a handful
of passes because the suction velocity head is about 1 % of the nozzle differential. The outer
solve is a 200-step bisection on the area ratio $b = A_t/A_m$.

**Which root, and why.** The outer equation has TWO roots — a small chamber with a large area
ratio, and a large one with a small ratio — and they are separated on a PHYSICAL ground rather
than a numerical one: the mixing-throat velocity. At the 322F001 duty the large-ratio root
puts 96 t/h of carbamate through the throat at 54 m/s, which is an erosion rate rather than an
operating point. The root taken gives 16.0 m/s, squarely in the 10-20 m/s band a liquid jet
pump is drawn for. The bracket ends below the other root, and both velocities are returned so
the choice can be re-checked rather than trusted.

**The model's falsifiable prediction of what is inside that scan:**

| | value |
|---|---|
| nozzle exit area $A_t$ | 0.00021959110412042918 m2, a 16.72 mm bore |
| mixing-throat area $A_m$ | 0.0019814767245892343 m2, a 50.23 mm bore |
| area ratio $b$ | 0.11082 |
| nozzle velocity | 89.44 m/s |
| throat velocity | 16.02 m/s |
| design $N$, $M_{vol}$ | 0.2019, 0.7185 |

## XXI.5 Agreement with the published N-M form

Non-dimensionalised at equal densities and zero losses, with $b = A_t/A_m$, $M = \dot m_s/\dot
m_p$ and $K = \dot m_p^2/(\rho A_m^2)$:

$$ \frac{p_d - p_s}{K} = \frac{1}{b} + \frac{M^2}{1-b} - \frac{M^2}{2(1-b)^2}
   - \frac{(1+M)^2}{2} $$

Multiplying by $2b^2$ gives the Cunningham / ESDU 85032 numerator of
$N = (p_d - p_s)/(p_p - p_d)$ term for term. The convention differs in the DENOMINATOR only:
the published form takes the nozzle velocity from the full $(p_p - p_s)$, putting the suction
acceleration entirely into the entry-loss coefficient, where the form here carries it
explicitly and lets the nozzle discharge into the actual throat-entry plane pressure. At the
322F001 duty the two differ by one suction velocity head — 0.27 bar against a 25 bar nozzle
differential, about 1 % — so the model is directly comparable with a published N-M curve, on
the published area convention.

**The loss coefficients are an open assumption, not a fit.** $K_n = 0.05$, $K_{en} = 0.10$,
$K_{th} = 0.05$ and $\eta_d = 0.80$ are representative values for a machined jet pump from the
open literature, applied uniformly — the same class of stated assumption as the generic globe
$F_L$ and $x_T$. They are not free parameters standing in for the design point, because the
geometry is back-solved THROUGH them: a different set moves the areas and leaves the design
duty exactly where it is. What it does move is the stall MARGIN, which is why that is a
handoff item and not a settled number.
